action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, a spreadsheet, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
1	# A10 Project Purpose Contract — FROZEN 2026-11-17
2	
3	Date drafted: 2026-11-17. Analyst: Matt Sorensen. AI role: Problem Setter, then Challenger (Claude Code, decision-statement-builder skill).
4	Source candidate: #1 in `report/A10_problem_scan_2026-11-17.md`.
5	Status: **FROZEN 2026-11-17, approved by Matt Sorensen.** This was done before any analysis of how inputs relate to the outcome; only structural profiling and join tests have been run. Any later change requires a dated amendment, added below, with a stated reason.
6	
7	## Contract fields
8	
9	| Field | Contract answer |
10	|---|---|
11	| **Purpose pathway** | **Predictive** (the one primary path). An explanatory layer reports how much director track record adds to the prediction. That's association only, with no causal claim. |
12	| **Decision** | At the financing stage, before production, the acquisitions team decides for each incoming project whether to **flag for deep review**, **proceed on standard review**, or **pass**. |
13	| **Action** | Each year, the 20% of projects with the highest predicted risk go to deep review (comparable-film analysis, a second reader, renegotiating terms). The rest get standard review. The screen never rejects a project on its own. |
14	| **Decision time** | When the financing decision is made, before production. **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, director's track record from earlier films only, production companies' track record from earlier films only, planned runtime, planned release month and quarter, original language, production country. **Prohibited inputs (known only after release):** revenue, box office, vote counts and averages, popularity, critic and audience scores, review text, TMDB keywords (crowd-edited after release). |
15	| **Population & unit** | Unit = **one feature film at its financing decision.** Population = feature films released 2000–2023 with a reported budget ≥ $1M and reported worldwide revenue > 0, excluding adult titles. Training: 2000–2015. Test: 2016–2019. Stress test: 2020–2023 (COVID era), reported separately. |
16	| **Outcome / target & horizon** | Positive class = **"money-loser": worldwide revenue < 2.5 × budget.** The 2.5× multiple is a labeled assumption (a commonly cited rule of thumb for covering marketing and the exhibitor's share). It's rerun at 1×, 2× and 3× as a sensitivity check. Horizon = full theatrical run as recorded in TMDB. The model estimates each project's probability of being a money-loser. |
17	| **Baseline** | (a) **Random 20% flagging**, which catches losers at the base rate (the floor). (b) **A simple rule:** flag projects in the genre × budget-tier groups with the highest historical loss rate, using training years only. The model has to beat (b), not just (a). |
18	| **Evidence standard** | On the 2016–2019 test films, the share of all money-losers that fall inside the flagged top 20% (capture rate). The model must beat rule (b) by **≥ 5 percentage points**, with a bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. Also report precision at 20%, calibration, and the result for the 2020–2023 stress set. *Bar confirmed by Matt at the freeze.* |
19	| **Value** | More money-losers reach deep review without adding review workload: same 20% capacity, better targeting. Value per year = (extra losers caught × loss avoided per caught loser × share of flagged deals actually changed) − (good films wrongly flagged × cost of a wrongly flagged deal). Each term is a **blank the owner fills in**; the report shows break-even values, not invented dollars. |
20	| **Constraints** | Review capacity: 20% of projects. Data rights: Kaggle public datasets, license recorded in the Data Receipt. Timing: frozen analysis by Nov 25, due Dec 4. No individual-level sensitive data, but director names are personal names, so results are reported at the aggregate or feature level, not as rankings of named people. Simplest adequate method: logistic regression first. |
21	| **Owner** | **Head of Acquisitions** at a representative film co-financier. This is a stand-in role: there are no real stakeholder interviews, and the report states that limitation. The owner is accountable for using the screen, monitoring it, and stopping it. |
22	
23	## Rival framing
24	**#2, director premium:** the greenlight committee decides whether to pay extra for a director with a strong track record. It uses the same data and time but asks a different question: what one input is worth, not sorting projects. It's the fallback if #1 fails the red-team or stop condition S1.
25	
26	## Prohibited uses
27	The screen must never quietly become:
28	1. **A tool for hiring or blacklisting people.** It must not rank, score or exclude individual directors or other talent, or feed into pay negotiations.
29	2. **An automatic reject.** A flag only sends a project to deep review, and a person makes the final call.
30	3. **A causal claim.** "Directors with strong track records *cause* profit" isn't supported. Track record is a predictive input and nothing more.
31	4. **A screen applied outside its population.** It doesn't cover micro-budget films (< $1M), streaming-only releases, or films without a theatrical revenue record.
32	
33	## Minimum evidence to move forward, and stop conditions
34	**Move to a pilot** (run alongside human review for one slate, with no decisions changed) only if S1 passes, calibration is acceptable on the test films, and capture on the 2020–2023 stress set doesn't fall below the rule baseline.
35	
36	| # | Stop trigger (observable) | Disposition |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| S1 | The model doesn't beat rule (b) by ≥ 5 pts of capture on 2016–2019 with a CI that excludes 0 | **Satisfice:** recommend the simple rule |
39	| S2 | Removing director track record changes capture by < 2 pts | Drop the director claim and report it as a null finding |
40	| S3 | The hand-check of 50 joined pairs shows > 10% wrong matches | Drop the RT join and use production-company track record as the focal factor |
41	| S4 | Films with a budget but no reported revenue are a large share of the population, and the cross-check with RT box office shows they skew toward losers | Restrict the claim to films with reported revenue, or **redirect** |
42	
43	## Red-team (Challenger)
44	
45	**Weakest link 1: a filter I set earlier selected on the outcome. *This is an AI correction.*** The "usable films" filter I used in the join tests required **≥ 50 TMDB votes**. Vote count is measured after release and rises with success (Spearman 0.48 with log ROI). Filtering on it silently drops obscure flops, which are exactly the films the screen exists to catch. That would make the loss rate look lower and the model look better than it is. **Fix:** the population now uses budget ≥ $1M and revenue > 0, with no vote filter (see above). This is a strong candidate for the report's required "material AI correction."
46	
47	**Weakest link 2: films with missing revenue.** 84,135 released TMDB films have a budget, but only 18,398 also have revenue. Films with no revenue on record are likely to include unreported flops. If so, the population is short on losers, and the base rate and capture will be biased. **Fix:** Phase 2 measures how many films have a budget ≥ $1M but no revenue, and uses RT domestic box office to estimate what those films earned (stop condition S4).
48

# A10 Project Purpose Contract — FROZEN 2026-11-17

Date drafted: 2026-11-17. Analyst: Matt Sorensen. AI role: Problem Setter, then Challenger (Claude Code, decision-statement-builder skill).
Source candidate: #1 in `report/A10_problem_scan_2026-11-17.md`.
Status: **FROZEN 2026-11-17, approved by Matt Sorensen.** This was done before any analysis of how inputs relate to the outcome; only structural profiling and join tests have been run. Any later change requires a dated amendment, added below, with a stated reason.

## Contract fields

| Field | Contract answer |
|---|---|
| **Purpose pathway** | **Predictive** (the one primary path). An explanatory layer reports how much director track record adds to the prediction. That's association only, with no causal claim. |
| **Decision** | At the financing stage, before production, the acquisitions team decides for each incoming project whether to **flag for deep review**, **proceed on standard review**, or **pass**. |
| **Action** | Each year, the 20% of projects with the highest predicted risk go to deep review (comparable-film analysis, a second reader, renegotiating terms). The rest get standard review. The screen never rejects a project on its own. |
| **Decision time** | When the financing decision is made, before production. **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, director's track record from earlier films only, production companies' track record from earlier films only, planned runtime, planned release month and quarter, original language, production country. **Prohibited inputs (known only after release):** revenue, box office, vote counts and averages, popularity, critic and audience scores, review text, TMDB keywords (crowd-edited after release). |
| **Population & unit** | Unit = **one feature film at its financing decision.** Population = feature films released 2000–2023 with a reported budget ≥ $1M and reported worldwide revenue > 0, excluding adult titles. Training: 2000–2015. Test: 2016–2019. Stress test: 2020–2023 (COVID era), reported separately. |
| **Outcome / target & horizon** | Positive class = **"money-loser": worldwide revenue < 2.5 × budget.** The 2.5× multiple is a labeled assumption (a commonly cited rule of thumb for covering marketing and the exhibitor's share). It's rerun at 1×, 2× and 3× as a sensitivity check. Horizon = full theatrical run as recorded in TMDB. The model estimates each project's probability of being a money-loser. |
| **Baseline** | (a) **Random 20% flagging**, which catches losers at the base rate (the floor). (b) **A simple rule:** flag projects in the genre × budget-tier groups with the highest historical loss rate, using training years only. The model has to beat (b), not just (a). |
| **Evidence standard** | On the 2016–2019 test films, the share of all money-losers that fall inside the flagged top 20% (capture rate). The model must beat rule (b) by **≥ 5 percentage points**, with a bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. Also report precision at 20%, calibration, and the result for the 2020–2023 stress set. *Bar confirmed by Matt at the freeze.* |
| **Value** | More money-losers reach deep review without adding review workload: same 20% capacity, better targeting. Value per year = (extra losers caught × loss avoided per caught loser × share of flagged deals actually changed) − (good films wrongly flagged × cost of a wrongly flagged deal). Each term is a **blank the owner fills in**; the report shows break-even values, not invented dollars. |
| **Constraints** | Review capacity: 20% of projects. Data rights: Kaggle public datasets, license recorded in the Data Receipt. Timing: frozen analysis by Nov 25, due Dec 4. No individual-level sensitive data, but director names are personal names, so results are reported at the aggregate or feature level, not as rankings of named people. Simplest adequate method: logistic regression first. |
| **Owner** | **Head of Acquisitions** at a representative film co-financier. This is a stand-in role: there are no real stakeholder interviews, and the report states that limitation. The owner is accountable for using the screen, monitoring it, and stopping it. |

## Rival framing
**#2, director premium:** the greenlight committee decides whether to pay extra for a director with a strong track record. It uses the same data and time but asks a different question: what one input is worth, not sorting projects. It's the fallback if #1 fails the red-team or stop condition S1.

## Prohibited uses
The screen must never quietly become:
1. **A tool for hiring or blacklisting people.** It must not rank, score or exclude individual directors or other talent, or feed into pay negotiations.
2. **An automatic reject.** A flag only sends a project to deep review, and a person makes the final call.
3. **A causal claim.** "Directors with strong track records *cause* profit" isn't supported. Track record is a predictive input and nothing more.
4. **A screen applied outside its population.** It doesn't cover micro-budget films (< $1M), streaming-only releases, or films without a theatrical revenue record.

## Minimum evidence to move forward, and stop conditions
**Move to a pilot** (run alongside human review for one slate, with no decisions changed) only if S1 passes, calibration is acceptable on the test films, and capture on the 2020–2023 stress set doesn't fall below the rule baseline.

| # | Stop trigger (observable) | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | The model doesn't beat rule (b) by ≥ 5 pts of capture on 2016–2019 with a CI that excludes 0 | **Satisfice:** recommend the simple rule |
| S2 | Removing director track record changes capture by < 2 pts | Drop the director claim and report it as a null finding |
| S3 | The hand-check of 50 joined pairs shows > 10% wrong matches | Drop the RT join and use production-company track record as the focal factor |
| S4 | Films with a budget but no reported revenue are a large share of the population, and the cross-check with RT box office shows they skew toward losers | Restrict the claim to films with reported revenue, or **redirect** |

## Red-team (Challenger)

**Weakest link 1: a filter I set earlier selected on the outcome. *This is an AI correction.*** The "usable films" filter I used in the join tests required **≥ 50 TMDB votes**. Vote count is measured after release and rises with success (Spearman 0.48 with log ROI). Filtering on it silently drops obscure flops, which are exactly the films the screen exists to catch. That would make the loss rate look lower and the model look better than it is. **Fix:** the population now uses budget ≥ $1M and revenue > 0, with no vote filter (see above). This is a strong candidate for the report's required "material AI correction."

**Weakest link 2: films with missing revenue.** 84,135 released TMDB films have a budget, but only 18,398 also have revenue. Films with no revenue on record are likely to include unreported flops. If so, the population is short on losers, and the base rate and capture will be biased. **Fix:** Phase 2 measures how many films have a budget ≥ $1M but no revenue, and uses RT domestic box office to estimate what those films earned (stop condition S4).

**Weakest link 3: is the value logic real?** Real financiers have scripts, cast packages, comparable films and presale data that a public-data screen doesn't. So could this ever beat their judgment? **Answer:** it isn't meant to replace their judgment. It's a base-rate check that decides where scarce deep-review time goes. The value claim is limited to "better targeting at the same capacity," and the report must say that we can't compare against the experts' actual track record, which isn't in the data.

**Weakest link 4: inputs that sit between "planned" and "actual."** TMDB records the *final* budget and runtime, not the planned ones, and they can drift during production, possibly more for troubled productions. That's a mild leak. **Fix:** report it as a limitation, and as a robustness check, refit using budget tiers rather than exact dollars.

**Did the dataset pick this problem?** Partly, and the scan flags it. Budget and revenue being available made this candidate feasible. The decision (where to spend limited review time) is still real and has an owner, so it stays, with the population limits stated openly.

**The course's five-question check**
1. *Predicting, changing, or describing?* Predicting: the risk of a loss at the financing stage. The director layer describes only, and nothing here claims to change outcomes.
2. *Where's the evidence and data receipt?* TMDB and the two RT files in `data/raw/`. The Data Receipt is plan step 8, still to do.
3. *What would make us stop, and would we recognize it?* S1–S4 above. Each one is a number checked against a stated threshold.
4. *Which CRISP-DM phase are we in?* Business Understanding. Only structural profiling has been done; no relationships with the outcome have been modeled.
5. *What exact quantity is being claimed?* The share of 2016–2019 money-losers (revenue < 2.5× budget) caught in the top 20% of predicted risk, compared with the genre × budget rule, with a 95% CI.

## Verification
- Every field has a specific answer: yes.
- Rival framing and prohibited uses are both present: yes.
- Stop conditions are observable triggers: yes, S1–S4.
- It has survived a real Challenger attack: four weak links were attacked, and one led to a change in the population definition.

## Freeze record
- [x] ≥ 5-point evidence bar confirmed by Matt, 2026-11-17.
- [x] $1M budget floor confirmed by Matt, 2026-11-17.
- [x] Instructor approval of the path: not required for this project (confirmed by Matt, 2026-11-17).

## Amendments
None yet.

3	Date drafted: 2026-11-17. Analyst: Matt Sorensen. AI role: Problem Setter, then Challenger (Claude Code, decision-statement-builder skill).

7	## Contract fields
8	
9	| Field | Contract answer |
10	|---|---|
11	| **Purpose pathway** | **Predictive** (the one primary path). An explanatory layer reports how much director track record adds to the prediction. That's association only, with no causal claim. |
12	| **Decision** | At the financing stage, before production, the acquisitions team decides for each incoming project whether to **flag for deep review**, **proceed on standard review**, or **pass**. |
13	| **Action** | Each year, the 20% of projects with the highest predicted risk go to deep review (comparable-film analysis, a second reader, renegotiating terms). The rest get standard review. The screen never rejects a project on its own. |
14	| **Decision time** | When the financing decision is made, before production. **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, director's track record from earlier films only, production companies' track record from earlier films only, planned runtime, planned release month and quarter, original language, production country. **Prohibited inputs (known only after release):** revenue, box office, vote counts and averages, popularity, critic and audience scores, review text, TMDB keywords (crowd-edited after release). |
15	| **Population & unit** | Unit = **one feature film at its financing decision.** Population = feature films released 2000–2023 with a reported budget ≥ $1M and reported worldwide revenue > 0, excluding adult titles. Training: 2000–2015. Test: 2016–2019. Stress test: 2020–2023 (COVID era), reported separately. |
16	| **Outcome / target & horizon** | Positive class = **"money-loser": worldwide revenue < 2.5 × budget.** The 2.5× multiple is a labeled assumption (a commonly cited rule of thumb for covering marketing and the exhibitor's share). It's rerun at 1×, 2× and 3× as a sensitivity check. Horizon = full theatrical run as recorded in TMDB. The model estimates each project's probability of being a money-loser. |
17	| **Baseline** | (a) **Random 20% flagging**, which catches losers at the base rate (the floor). (b) **A simple rule:** flag projects in the genre × budget-tier groups with the highest historical loss rate, using training years only. The model has to beat (b), not just (a). |
18	| **Evidence standard** | On the 2016–2019 test films, the share of all money-losers that fall inside the flagged top 20% (capture rate). The model must beat rule (b) by **≥ 5 percentage points**, with a bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. Also report precision at 20%, calibration, and the result for the 2020–2023 stress set. *Bar confirmed by Matt at the freeze.* |
19	| **Value** | More money-losers reach deep review without adding review workload: same 20% capacity, better targeting. Value per year = (extra losers caught × loss avoided per caught loser × share of flagged deals actually changed) − (good films wrongly flagged × cost of a wrongly flagged deal). Each term is a **blank the owner fills in**; the report shows break-even values, not invented dollars. |
20	| **Constraints** | Review capacity: 20% of projects. Data rights: Kaggle public datasets, license recorded in the Data Receipt. Timing: frozen analysis by Nov 25, due Dec 4. No individual-level sensitive data, but director names are personal names, so results are reported at the aggregate or feature level, not as rankings of named people. Simplest adequate method: logistic regression first. |
21	| **Owner** | **Head of Acquisitions** at a representative film co-financier. This is a stand-in role: there are no real stakeholder interviews, and the report states that limitation. The owner is accountable for using the screen, monitoring it, and stopping it. |
22	
23	## Rival framing
24	**#2, director premium:** the greenlight committee decides whether to pay extra for a director with a strong track record. It uses the same data and time but asks a different question: what one input is worth, not sorting projects. It's the fallback if #1 fails the red-team or stop condition S1.
25	
26	## Prohibited uses
27	The screen must never quietly become:
28	1. **A tool for hiring or blacklisting people.** It must not rank, score or exclude individual directors or other talent, or feed into pay negotiations.
29	2. **An automatic reject.** A flag only sends a project to deep review, and a person makes the final call.
30	3. **A causal claim.** "Directors with strong track records *cause* profit" isn't supported. Track record is a predictive input and nothing more.
31	4. **A screen applied outside its population.** It doesn't cover micro-budget films (< $1M), streaming-only releases, or films without a theatrical revenue record.
32	
33	## Minimum evidence to move forward, and stop conditions
34	**Move to a pilot** (run alongside human review for one slate, with no decisions changed) only if S1 passes, calibration is acceptable on the test films, and capture on the 2020–2023 stress set doesn't fall below the rule baseline.
35	
36	| # | Stop trigger (observable) | Disposition |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| S1 | The model doesn't beat rule (b) by ≥ 5 pts of capture on 2016–2019 with a CI that excludes 0 | **Satisfice:** recommend the simple rule |
39	| S2 | Removing director track record changes capture by < 2 pts | Drop the director claim and report it as a null finding |
40	| S3 | The hand-check of 50 joined pairs shows > 10% wrong matches | Drop the RT join and use production-company track record as the focal factor |
41	| S4 | Films with a budget but no reported revenue are a large share of the population, and the cross-check with RT box office shows they skew toward losers | Restrict the claim to films with reported revenue, or **redirect** |
42	
43	## Red-team (Challenger)
44	
45	**Weakest link 1: a filter I set earlier selected on the outcome. *This is an AI correction.*** The "usable films" filter I used in the join tests required **≥ 50 TMDB votes**. Vote count is measured after release and rises with success (Spearman 0.48 with log ROI). Filtering on it silently drops obscure flops, which are exactly the films the screen exists to catch. That would make the loss rate look lower and the model look better than it is. **Fix:** the population now uses budget ≥ $1M and revenue > 0, with no vote filter (see above). This is a strong candidate for the report's required "material AI correction."
46	
47	**Weakest link 2: films with missing revenue.** 84,135 released TMDB films have a budget, but only 18,398 also have revenue. Films with no revenue on record are likely to include unreported flops. If so, the population is short on losers, and the base rate and capture will be biased. **Fix:** Phase 2 measures how many films have a budget ≥ $1M but no revenue, and uses RT domestic box office to estimate what those films earned (stop condition S4).
48	
49	**Weakest link 3: is the value logic real?** Real financiers have scripts, cast packages, comparable films and presale data that a public-data screen doesn't. So could this ever beat their judgment? **Answer:** it isn't meant to replace their judgment. It's a base-rate check that decides where scarce deep-review time goes. The value claim is limited to "better targeting at the same capacity," and the report must say that we can't compare against the experts' actual track record, which isn't in the data.
50	
51	**Weakest link 4: inputs that sit between "planned" and "actual."** TMDB records the *final* budget and runtime, not the planned ones, and they can drift during production, possibly more for troubled productions. That's a mild leak. **Fix:** report it as a limitation, and as a robustness check, refit using budget tiers rather than exact dollars.
52	
53	**Did the dataset pick this problem?** Partly, and the scan flags it. Budget and revenue being available made this candidate feasible. The decision (where to spend limited review time) is still real and has an owner, so it stays, with the population limits stated openly.
54	
55	**The course's five-question check**
56	1. *Predicting, changing, or describing?* Predicting: the risk of a loss at the financing stage. The director layer describes only, and nothing here claims to change outcomes.
57	2. *Where's the evidence and data receipt?* TMDB and the two RT files in `data/raw/`. The Data Receipt is plan step 8, still to do.

59	4. *Which CRISP-DM phase are we in?* Business Understanding. Only structural profiling has been done; no relationships with the outcome have been modeled.
60	5. *What exact quantity is being claimed?* The share of 2016–2019 money-losers (revenue < 2.5× budget) caught in the top 20% of predicted risk, compared with the genre × budget rule, with a 95% CI.

I read the README (one line) and both A10 docs. Here's what we're working on.

## The project
This is the A10 team project for EMBA 560. It's due **Fri Dec 4, 2026 at 3:30 PM** and is worth 120 points. Matt Sorensen wrote both docs. I'm guessing you're the "one colleague" in the plan.

**The question:** Can a model built only on information available before production flag which film projects are likely to lose money, better than a simple rule can?

- **Decision owner:** a stand-in Head of Acquisitions at a film co-financier. For each project at the financing stage, they choose deep review, standard review or pass.
- **Action:** the riskiest 20% of projects get deep review. The screen never rejects a project on its own.
- **Target:** "money-loser" means worldwide revenue is less than 2.5× budget. The 2.5× is an assumption, so it gets rerun at 1×, 2× and 3×.
- **Population:** films released 2000–2023 with a budget of at least $1M and revenue above $0, excluding adult titles. There's **no vote-count filter**. That filter was removed as an AI correction because vote count is measured after release and leaks the outcome.
- **Split:** train on 2000–2015, test on 2016–2019, and run a separate stress test on 2020–2023 (the COVID years).
- **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, runtime, release month and quarter, language, country, and the track records of the director and production companies from earlier films only. Anything measured after release is off-limits: revenue, votes, popularity, scores, reviews and keywords.
- **What counts as success:** logistic regression has to catch at least 5 percentage points more of the 2016–2019 money-losers in its top 20% than the genre × budget-tier rule does. That's called the capture rate. The bootstrap 95% CI also has to exclude 0.
- **Stop conditions:**
  - S1: the model misses that bar, so we recommend the simple rule instead.
  - S2: removing director track record changes capture by less than 2 points, so the director claim is reported as a null finding.
  - S3: more than 10% of the joined title pairs we hand-check are wrong matches, so we drop the RT join.
  - S4: films with a budget but no reported revenue skew toward losers, so the claim gets narrowed.
- **Data:** a TMDB dataset of 1.54M rows, plus Rotten Tomatoes (RT) reviews and movies files from Kaggle. The title+year join matched about 80% of films. The RT movies file also adds director names.

## Where the plan stands
- **Phase 0 (setup):** done. Splitting the work between you and Matt was deferred, and the plan treats Matt as owning everything for now.
- **Phase 1 (purpose contract):** done. The contract was frozen on Nov 17. Step 7 is still unchecked in the plan, but the contract file says it's frozen, so the checklist is just out of date.
- **Phase 2 (Data Receipt and data understanding, Nov 19–21):** should be underway, but nothing is checked off. This covers recording each source, profiling every field, verifying the join with a 50-pair hand-check, and the S4 check on missing revenue.
- **Phases 3–4 (preparation and modeling):** must be finished by **Nov 25**. The plan says that if work runs behind, the second model and the early-buzz feature get cut first.

## What's in this repo and what isn't
- There's only a README and these two docs.
- None of the folders from the plan are here: `data/raw`, `notebooks/`, `ai_logs/`, `report/`.
- The CSVs, the problem scan report and Matt's notebook aren't here either. The paths in the plan point to Matt's Windows machine.
- The plan also has some stale bits. Its "Direction" section still describes the old filter (budget ≥ $100K and at least 50 votes, about 7,716 films), which the frozen contract replaced.

**What's your role, and what do you want to tackle first?** Some options:
1. Set up the folder layout here and pull in the data.
2. Start Phase 2 work (Data Receipt, profiling, verifying the join).
3. Do an independent rebuild as your own track. Appendix D asks for an independent rebuild of 3–5 key numbers.

Also, are the data files somewhere I can get to, or do they need to be downloaded from Kaggle?

"""Download the A10 raw datasets from Kaggle into data/raw/.

Run from the repo root:  python tools/get_data.py
Files are gitignored; every collaborator runs this once on their own machine.
data/raw/ is treated as read-only after download — never edit these files.
"""
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

import kagglehub

RAW = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "raw"

# Kaggle handle -> files expected from it (recorded in the Data Receipt)
DATASETS = {
    "asaniczka/tmdb-movies-dataset-2023-930k-movies": ["TMDB_movie_dataset_v11.csv"],
    "priyamchoksi/rotten-tomato-movie-reviews-1-44m-rows": ["rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv"],
    "andrezaza/clapper-massive-rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-reviews": ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv"],
}


def main() -> None:
    RAW.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for handle, wanted in DATASETS.items():
        print(f"\n== {handle}")
        src = Path(kagglehub.dataset_download(handle))
        for name in wanted:
            dst = RAW / name
            if dst.exists():
                print(f"  exists, skipping: {dst.name}")
                continue
            matches = list(src.rglob(name))
            if not matches:
                available = sorted(p.name for p in src.rglob("*") if p.is_file())
                print(f"  NOT FOUND: {name}. Files in download: {available}")
                continue
            shutil.copy2(matches[0], dst)
            print(f"  copied {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

---
name: zscaler-python-ssl
description: Tanner's Mac sits behind Cricut's Zscaler TLS proxy; Python HTTPS (kagglehub, requests) fails cert verification unless truststore is used
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Cricut's Zscaler proxy re-signs HTTPS traffic. curl works because it uses the macOS keychain, but Python fails with `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`.

**How to apply:** in Python scripts that download data, `import truststore; truststore.inject_into_ssl()` before importing kagglehub/requests. The EMBA 560 A10 repo's `tools/get_data.py` already does this.

I created both notebooks, and your notebook ran from start to finish with no errors.

- **`notebooks/A10-master.ipynb`** has only a title cell. It's where the final shared work will be merged from both your notebooks.
- **`notebooks/Edwards-A10.ipynb`** has the imports and loads all five files. It profiles every column (type, % missing, distinct values) and checks Matt's numbers. It only describes the data's structure: the contract says not to look at how inputs relate to the outcome until features are built.

## Matt's numbers check out
| Check | Matt's figure | Mine |
|---|---|---|
| Released films with budget > 0 | 84,135 | **84,135** ✓ |
| …that also have revenue > 0 | 18,398 | **18,398** ✓ |
| RT movies rows / duplicate ids | 143,258 / 1,206 | **143,258 / 1,206** ✓ |

So the head start is solid on these numbers.

## Three new findings
1. **S4 may be triggered.** The contract population is **5,766 films**. Another **4,455 films** have a budget of at least $1M but no revenue on record, which is 44% of all films with that budget. Stop condition S4 kicks in when this group is "a large share" *and* it skews toward money-losers. The first half looks met. The second half needs the cross-check against RT box office. That should be the next validation, because a failure means narrowing the claim or redirecting the project.
2. **TMDB has 1,407 duplicate film ids.** The plan doesn't mention them. They need a line in the cleaning ledger, and I haven't checked yet how many are inside the population.

The notebook also flags 34,165 placeholder budgets under $1,000 and 374K missing release dates. Those go in the cleaning ledger later.

## Setup (once per machine)

Requires Python 3.12. [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is recommended, but plain `venv` + `pip` works too.

```bash
# 1. Environment
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv -r requirements.txt
#   Windows without uv:  py -3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv\Scripts\pip install -r requirements.txt

# 2. Strip notebook outputs on commit (git filter config is local; each person must run this)
.venv/bin/nbstripout --install          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\nbstripout --install

# 3. Download raw data from Kaggle into data/raw/ (about 1.3 GB, gitignored)
.venv/bin/python tools/get_data.py      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\python tools\get_data.py
```

Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy (e.g. Zscaler), `get_data.py` uses `truststore` so Python trusts the OS certificate store.

|---|---|---|

content.text:
I've **added** the Box Office Mojo file rather than replacing anything. It's in `get_data.py`, the README's data sources table and your notebook, and the notebook still runs from start to finish.

**Why it can't replace anything:** it only has **domestic (US) grosses**. The contract's target is worldwide revenue against budget, so TMDB stays the core source. What this file *can* do is give an independent check on revenue, alongside the RT `boxOffice` column. It has two advantages there: daily data with dates, and coverage from 2000 to Jan 2025.

**What I found:**
- 356K rows, one per film per day, covering **7,176 titles**.
- The `id` column is unique for **every row**, so it can't be used as a film key. The only way to join is on title + year.
- A quick title + year (±1) match links **59% of the contract population** (3,387 of 5,766 films).
- **Early S4 signal:** only **4%** of the 4,455 films with a budget but no revenue (187 films) show up in Box Office Mojo at all. That suggests most of them never had a tracked US theatrical release, rather than being hidden flops. If that holds up, many of them are outside the population anyway (prohibited use #4 excludes films with no theatrical revenue record). That's good news for S4. But this was a rough match with no hand-check, so treat it as a lead, not a finding.

**For the Data Receipt:** the data was scraped from Box Office Mojo, which IMDb owns, and published through a personal GitHub repo. It has no Kaggle-style license, so the report should say that.

Still waiting on your call: **should I commit the setup, both notebooks and this addition?** Then I'll do the full S4 check next, using both Box Office Mojo and the RT box office data.

content.text:
I checked this before recommending anything. TMDB's financial data is missing **unevenly**, and that matters more than how much is missing.

**TMDB coverage for the 5,866 US theatrical releases (2000–2023) I could match** (86% of Box Office Mojo's titles):

| Domestic gross | Films | Has budget | Has budget + revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| under $1M | 2,077 | 26% | **18%** |
| $1–10M | 1,064 | 61% | 56% |
| $10–50M | 1,491 | 90% | 87% |
| $50M+ | 1,234 | 98% | 97% |

So TMDB covers films that did well and is missing the small films that flopped. Those are the money-losers the screen is supposed to catch. This is S4's worry, now with evidence: the population as defined has too few losers.

**Switching to US domestic only doesn't fix this.** The bottleneck is **budget**, not revenue. A money-loser is defined by revenue relative to budget, and neither Box Office Mojo nor RT has budgets. With domestic-only data we'd still get budgets from TMDB, with the same gap. We'd also lose the worldwide revenue that the 2.5× rule is based on.

**Realistic options:**
1. **Find a better budget source.** The Numbers (the-numbers.com) is the industry-standard public budget list, about 6,000 films, with domestic and worldwide grosses, and Kaggle has scraped copies. It probably shares the same bias (studios disclose budgets for bigger films), but it would fill some gaps and gives an independent check on TMDB's figures.
2. **Narrow the claim.** S4 already plans for this: "restrict the claim to films with reported revenue." The screen would cover films with disclosed budgets, and the report would use the Box Office Mojo table above to show exactly how that population is skewed. It would need a dated amendment to the frozen contract.
3. **Change the target to something that doesn't need budget**, for example "domestic gross under $X." That changes the decision itself, which is close to starting over 13 days before the deadline.

**My recommendation: option 1 to see how much it helps, then option 2 for whatever gap is left.** Either way, the coverage table above is strong material for the report. It turns S4 from a guess into a measured finding.

Do you want me to look for a The Numbers dataset on Kaggle, or do you already have one in mind? Also, because this touches the frozen contract, you'll probably want Matt's agreement before any amendment. I haven't changed anything yet.
