WORDS = {"two": "2", "three": "3", "four": "4", "eight": "8", "sixty": "60"}
FILLER = {"the", "a", "an", "part", "episode", "movie"}


def loose_title(x) -> str:
    """Looser key for The Numbers' title style: 'Star Wars Ep. III', 'Ocean's 8', 'Dr. Seuss' The Grinch', truncated '…'."""
    x = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", str(x)).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode().lower()
    x = x.replace("&", " and ").replace("...", " ")
    x = re.sub(r"\(.*?\)|\[.*?\]", " ", x)                      # parentheticals: foreign titles, '(2016)'
    x = re.sub(r"^(disney|dr\.? seuss|tyler perry|marvel)\S*\s+", "", x)   # possessive brand prefixes
    x = re.sub(r"\b3-?d\b|\bimax\b", " ", x)
    x = re.sub(r"\bep\b\.?", "episode", x)
    toks = [ROMAN.get(t, WORDS.get(t, t)) for t in re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", x).split()]
    return " ".join(t for t in toks if t not in FILLER)


def title_score(a_raw, b_raw):
    a, b = loose_title(a_raw), loose_title(b_raw)
    s = difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, a, b).ratio()
    if "…" in str(a_raw) and b.startswith(a):                  # The Numbers truncates long titles
        s = max(s, 0.99)
    if min(len(a), len(b)) >= 6 and (a in b or b in a):        # subtitle added/dropped
        s = max(s, 0.9)
    return s

# runtime is within 10 min (or unknown); a year difference needs runtime within 5.
un = tn.drop(index=tn_match["src_row"])
free = tmdb.loc[~tmdb["id"].isin(tn_match["id"]) & tmdb["budget"].gt(0), ["id", "title", "original_title", "year", "runtime", "budget"]]
cands = []
for i, r in un.iterrows():
    b = r["Production Budget (USD)"]
    if not b > 0:
        continue
    c = free[(free["year"] - r["year"]).abs().le(1) & ((free["budget"] / b - 1).abs() < 0.15)]
    for _, s in c.iterrows():

print(f"Second pass matched {len(c2)} more The Numbers films (total {len(tn_match):,} of {len(tn):,})")

This pass matches the leftovers to TMDB films not already claimed:

1. **Loose title key:** drops parentheticals, brand prefixes (*Disney's*, *Dr. Seuss'*, *Tyler Perry's*), "3D", filler words (the, part, episode, movie); Roman numerals and number words become digits. Similarity score 0–1; a truncated or subtitle-dropped title that fits inside the other counts as a match.
2. **Year within ±1** and **money agrees**, either:
   - **A:** budget within 15%, score ≥ 0.85, runtime within 10 min (5 if the years differ), or

=== md cell 0
# A10: Data Understanding on the unified dataset (Tanner Edwards)

Personal notebook. Re-runs Matt's Data Understanding (`Sorensen-A10.ipynb` §2–§3, plan steps 8–9) on the **unified dataset** built by `00_build_dataset.ipynb`, which adds four sources and grows the usable population from 5,766 to about 6,900 films. Same helpers, same review flags, same privacy rule.

**Run `00_build_dataset.ipynb` first.** This notebook only reads `data/clean/films_unified.csv` and the raw files; it writes nothing.

| Section | What | Matt's equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Setup and Matt's profile helpers | §1, §3 helpers |
| 2 | Data Receipt for the **new** sources | §2 |
| 3a | Field inventory: all columns, role at the financing decision | §3a |
| 3b | The label on the expanded population | §3b |
| 3c–3f | Numeric, categorical, identifier/text and date fields | §3c–§3h |
| 3g | **New:** do the sources agree with each other? | — |
| 3h | **New:** who has which data (coverage by period and budget tier) | §4a idea |
| 3i | Flag register | §3i |
| 3j–3k | Findings and proposed dispositions (need Tanner + Matt sign-off) | §3j–§3k |

This section **observes and records; it doesn't clean.**

=== md cell 5
## 2. Data Receipt for the new sources (plan step 8)

Matt's §2 covers TMDB, RT movies (andrezaza) and RT reviews. These are the sources added since. Licenses were read from the Kaggle API (`licenseName`) and the GitHub API on 2026-11-23.

| Field | The Numbers | Box Office Mojo | Wikidata snapshot | RT movies (stefanoleone992) | RT critic reviews (stefanoleone992) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **File** | `the_numbers/Top Movies (Cleaned Data).csv` | `boxofficemojo/revenues_per_day.csv.gz` | `wikidata/wikidata_film_financials_2026-11-21.csv` | `stefanoleone992/rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv` | `stefanoleone992/rotten_tomatoes_critic_reviews.csv` |
| **Publisher** | michaelmatta0 (Kaggle) | tjwaterman99 (GitHub release) | Our own SPARQL query (`tools/wikidata_films.rq`) | stefanoleone992 (Kaggle) | same |
| **Original source** | the-numbers.com (Nash Information Services) | boxofficemojo.com (IMDb) | Wikidata (Wikimedia, crowd-edited) | Rotten Tomatoes | Rotten Tomatoes |
| **URL** | kaggle.com/datasets/michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata | github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper | query.wikidata.org | kaggle.com/datasets/stefanoleone992/rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-critic-reviews-dataset | same |
| **Access date** | 2026-11-21 | 2026-11-20 | 2026-11-21 (snapshot committed to git) | 2026-11-20 | 2026-11-20 |
| **License (as stated)** | MIT | **None stated** | CC0 1.0 | CC0 1.0 | CC0 1.0 |
| **Claimed grain** | One row per film | One row per film **per day** | One row per film with a USD budget and a TMDB id | One row per RT film (link) | One row per critic review |
| **Population** | ~6.6k "top" films by budget, all years | Films on the US daily chart, 2000–2025 | Wikidata films 2000–2023 with a USD cost | ~17.7k RT films (2020 scrape) | Reviews of those films |
| **Sensitive fields** | None | None | None | `directors`, `authors`, `actors`: public professionals | `critic_name`, `review_content`: named people and copyrighted text |
| **Rights caveats** | Scraped; The Numbers' terms aren't overridden by the uploader's MIT | Scraped; no license, so academic fair use only | — | Scores belong to RT | Review text is copyrighted; not copied into the unified file |
| **Permitted use here** | Academic, non-commercial. Cite the-numbers.com. | Same, and cite Box Office Mojo | Cite Wikidata | Same as Matt's RT files | Same; counts only |

**Also note:** `get_data.py` downloads `rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv` from **priyamchoksi** (license MIT), while Matt's receipt cites the **andrezaza** upload (CC0). Same row count (1,444,963). The receipt should cite one; open question for Matt.

=== md cell 14
## 3. Univariate profile of every field (plan step 9)

**Which rows:** the usable films (2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0 from any source), the population the screen will score. The label is shown by period. **Review flags (Ch 6):** |skew| > 0.5; any category level held by < 5% of non-missing rows. **Privacy:** director, writer, actor and critic names are profiled by counts only.

=== md cell 18
### 3b. The label on the expanded population
Money-loser = combined revenue < 2.5 × combined budget, with 1×, 2×, 3× sensitivity. Compared with Matt's TMDB-only figures (64.6% losers overall), and split by where the financials came from.

=== md cell 22
### 3d. Categorical fields
Multi-label fields are split on commas, so shares add to more than 100%. Person fields (director, writer, actors) show counts only.

=== md cell 28
### 3g. Do the sources agree? (new)

Where two sources report the same thing, they should agree. Disagreement is either a wrong match or a data error, and it tells Phase 3 which source to trust. Agreement = within 15% for money, 5 minutes for runtime, 7 days for release dates, same label for MPAA.

=== md cell 30
### 3h. Who has which data? (new)
Matt found the RT join covers big films better than small ones (58% of $1–5M vs 91% of $60M+). The same check for every source and key input, by period and budget tier. Uneven coverage means missing values aren't random, so Phase 3 needs "unknown" indicators, not dropped rows.

=== md cell 34
### 3j. What the profile shows (facts from the outputs above, run 2026-11-23)

**Population and the label**
1. **6,928 usable films** (train 5,020 · test 1,281 · stress 627), up from Matt's 5,766. The test set grows 18% (1,086 → 1,281), which tightens the bootstrap CI on the evidence standard.
2. **The added films are mostly losers.** Films whose budget or revenue came from The Numbers or Wikidata are 79% losers at 2.5×, against 65% for Matt's TMDB-only films. Overall: 67.1% (Matt 64.6%). This is the S4 worry in reverse: the extra sources recover some of the flops TMDB was missing. The 20%-capacity ceiling drops slightly, from 31% to 30% of losers.
3. **S4 is still triggered.** 38.7% of films with a budget ≥ $1M still have no revenue from any source (Matt: 43.6%), and 52% in the stress years.
4. **Junk values grew with the population.** 268 films earn < 1% of budget (Matt 179), 35 report revenue < $1,000, 379 < $100,000. The lowest are the same junk Matt found (*Aquajots*: $100M budget, $1 revenue). Six films above 100×, including *Vacancy* (2018, $903M on $1M) and a new one, *Space Station 3D*, where a Wikidata budget meets a TMDB revenue.

**Do the sources agree?** (new)
5. **Money mostly agrees.** Budget: TMDB vs The Numbers 85%, TMDB vs Wikidata 90% (within 15%). Worldwide revenue: 81–87%. Domestic gross across The Numbers, Box Office Mojo and RT: 92–97%. Runtime: 92–93% within 5 minutes. MPAA rating: the three sources agree on 99%.
6. **Release dates often don't.** TMDB's date is within 7 days of The Numbers / Box Office Mojo for only 74–75% of films. TMDB often records the first release anywhere (a festival or a foreign market); the others record the US release. Release month is an allowed input, so Phase 3 has to pick one definition.
7. **Matt's domestic-as-worldwide risk is larger than first counted:** 434 films (Matt: 396) have TMDB revenue equal to RT domestic. **The Numbers has a higher worldwide figure for 220 of them**, a direct repair.

**Coverage is uneven** (new)
8. **Every extra source covers big films far better than small ones.** The Numbers matches 36% of $1–5M films vs 88% of $60M+; MPAA and source material 34–35% vs 88%; director 61% vs 88%; franchise 3% vs 42%. Small films are where most losers are, so a missing value is not random. RT stefanoleone992 (scraped in 2020) has actors for only 5% of stress-period films.
9. **Franchise is thin and partly garbled:** 14% coverage; 92 of 1,004 values look like several franchise names run together (e.g. "BatmanDark Knight Trilogy").
10. **Track records are sparse:** 63% of directors and 67% of production companies appear in only one usable film.

**Keys and duplicates**
11. **Duplicates (fixed in the build, 2026-11-23).** The first profile found title+year pairs that were the same film entered twice (*Spider-Man: No Way Home*, *Timber Falls*): the build's rule required runtime within 5 minutes, and one copy had runtime 0. The rule now treats 0 as unknown, which also caught *WALL·E* and *Black Panther: Wakanda Forever*. 3 pairs remain and are **not** duplicates: *Underdogs* (two different 2013 films), *Uncharted 2* (a video game, entered twice) and a junk *Blue Beetle* entry ($400M revenue, runtime 0). Those are cleaning issues. 2 usable films share a Wikidata item.
12. **Review duplicates (fixed in the build).** The stefanoleone992 review file had 120,945 exact duplicate rows and the andrezaza file 12,394 repeated review ids; both are dropped before the rollups.

**Raw-file notes:** The Numbers has 150 release dates after the access date (up to 2068); none reach the usable population. RT sl reviews have 83 placeholder dates (1800-01-01). The Box Office Mojo scraper has no license.

=== md cell 35
### 3k. Proposed dispositions and phase gate (DRAFT, pending Tanner + Matt sign-off)

Matt's §3k rows 1–12 still apply. These are the additions for the unified dataset. **None are applied here.**

| # | Flag | Evidence | Proposed disposition | Treatment | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U1 | Population now multi-source | 6,931 films; 1,168 use The Numbers / Wikidata financials | Requires a contract amendment | Dated amendment: population = 2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0 **from TMDB, The Numbers or Wikidata**, with source precedence stated | Amendment recorded in the contract file |
| U2 | Added films skew to losers | 79% vs 65% losers | Usable; report it | Report results on the full population and on Matt's TMDB-only population as a sensitivity check | Capture on both populations |
| U3 | Domestic-as-worldwide revenue | 434 films; The Numbers higher for 220 | Requires repair | Replace TMDB revenue with The Numbers worldwide where TMDB = RT domestic and The Numbers is higher. Flag the other 214. | Loser rate before / after |
| U4 | Source disagreement on budget / revenue | 81–90% agree within 15% | Requires a rule | Keep precedence TMDB → The Numbers → Wikidata, but hand-check films where they disagree by > 2× | Hand-check sample error rate |
| U5 | Release date definitions differ | 74% agree within 7 days | Requires a rule | Use the US release date (The Numbers / Box Office Mojo) where available, TMDB otherwise; keep the source | Month distribution before / after |
| U6 | Coverage skews by budget | The Numbers 36% vs 88%; director 61% vs 88% | Usable with a limitation | Every optional input gets an "unknown" indicator; no dropped rows | Loser rate by known / unknown |
| U7 | Leftover duplicates | Runtime 0 blocked the merge rule | **Done** (build, 2026-11-23) | Runtime 0 counts as unknown; 4 more films merged | 3 same-title pairs left, none duplicates |
| U8 | Review duplicates | 120,945 + 12,394 duplicate reviews | **Done** (build, 2026-11-23) | Dropped before the rollups | Counts reported in the build |
| U11 | Junk entries | *Uncharted 2* (video game), *Blue Beetle* copy with $400M revenue and runtime 0 | Requires repair | Cleaning rule for runtime-0 TMDB entries that collide with a real film | Pair count after cleaning |
| U9 | Franchise field | 14% coverage, 92 garbled values | Investigate | See `FEATURE_IDEAS.md` (sequel / franchise); likely needs Wikidata series data | Coverage after |
| U10 | Candidate inputs not in the contract | MPAA, source, creative type, writer, cast, franchise | Needs a decision | Decide which to add by amendment before Phase 3 features | Decision recorded |

**Proposed phase gate: CONTINUE**, after U1 (amendment). Build fixes U7 and U8 are done. The S4 readiness verdict still belongs to step 12.

| **Publisher** | michaelmatta0 (Kaggle) | tjwaterman99 (GitHub release) | Our own SPARQL query (`tools/wikidata_films.rq`) | stefanoleone992 (Kaggle) | same |
| **Original source** | the-numbers.com (Nash Information Services) | boxofficemojo.com (IMDb) | Wikidata (Wikimedia, crowd-edited) | Rotten Tomatoes | Rotten Tomatoes |
| **URL** | kaggle.com/datasets/michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata | github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper | query.wikidata.org | kaggle.com/datasets/stefanoleone992/rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-critic-reviews-dataset | same |
| **Access date** | 2026-11-21 | 2026-11-20 | 2026-11-21 (snapshot committed to git) | 2026-11-20 | 2026-11-20 |
| **License (as stated)** | MIT | **None stated** | CC0 1.0 | CC0 1.0 | CC0 1.0 |
| **Claimed grain** | One row per film | One row per film **per day** | One row per film with a USD budget and a TMDB id | One row per RT film (link) | One row per critic review |
| **Population** | ~6.6k "top" films by budget, all years | Films on the US daily chart, 2000–2025 | Wikidata films 2000–2023 with a USD cost | ~17.7k RT films (2020 scrape) | Reviews of those films |
| **Sensitive fields** | None | None | None | `directors`, `authors`, `actors`: public professionals | `critic_name`, `review_content`: named people and copyrighted text |
| **Rights caveats** | Scraped; The Numbers' terms aren't overridden by the uploader's MIT | Scraped; no license, so academic fair use only | — | Scores belong to RT | Review text is copyrighted; not copied into the unified file |
| **Permitted use here** | Academic, non-commercial. Cite the-numbers.com. | Same, and cite Box Office Mojo | Cite Wikidata | Same as Matt's RT files | Same; counts only |

**Also note:** `get_data.py` downloads `rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv` from **priyamchoksi** (license MIT), while Matt's receipt cites the **andrezaza** upload (CC0). Same row count (1,444,963). The receipt should cite one; open question for Matt.

=== md cell 14
## 3. Univariate profile of every field (plan step 9)

**Which rows:** the usable films (2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0 from any source), the population the screen will score. The label is shown by period. **Review flags (Ch 6):** |skew| > 0.5; any category level held by < 5% of non-missing rows. **Privacy:** director, writer, actor and critic names are profiled by counts only.

=== md cell 18
### 3b. The label on the expanded population
Money-loser = combined revenue < 2.5 × combined budget, with 1×, 2×, 3× sensitivity. Compared with Matt's TMDB-only figures (64.6% losers overall), and split by where the financials came from.

=== md cell 22
### 3d. Categorical fields
Multi-label fields are split on commas, so shares add to more than 100%. Person fields (director, writer, actors) show counts only.

=== md cell 28
### 3g. Do the sources agree? (new)

Where two sources report the same thing, they should agree. Disagreement is either a wrong match or a data error, and it tells Phase 3 which source to trust. Agreement = within 15% for money, 5 minutes for runtime, 7 days for release dates, same label for MPAA.

=== md cell 30
### 3h. Who has which data? (new)
Matt found the RT join covers big films better than small ones (58% of $1–5M vs 91% of $60M+). The same check for every source and key input, by period and budget tier. Uneven coverage means missing values aren't random, so Phase 3 needs "unknown" indicators, not dropped rows.

=== md cell 34
### 3j. What the profile shows (facts from the outputs above, run 2026-11-23)

**Population and the label**
1. **6,928 usable films** (train 5,020 · test 1,281 · stress 627), up from Matt's 5,766. The test set grows 18% (1,086 → 1,281), which tightens the bootstrap CI on the evidence standard.
2. **The added films are mostly losers.** Films whose budget or revenue came from The Numbers or Wikidata are 79% losers at 2.5×, against 65% for Matt's TMDB-only films. Overall: 67.1% (Matt 64.6%). This is the S4 worry in reverse: the extra sources recover some of the flops TMDB was missing. The 20%-capacity ceiling drops slightly, from 31% to 30% of losers.
3. **S4 is still triggered.** 38.7% of films with a budget ≥ $1M still have no revenue from any source (Matt: 43.6%), and 52% in the stress years.
4. **Junk values grew with the population.** 268 films earn < 1% of budget (Matt 179), 35 report revenue < $1,000, 379 < $100,000. The lowest are the same junk Matt found (*Aquajots*: $100M budget, $1 revenue). Six films above 100×, including *Vacancy* (2018, $903M on $1M) and a new one, *Space Station 3D*, where a Wikidata budget meets a TMDB revenue.

**Do the sources agree?** (new)
5. **Money mostly agrees.** Budget: TMDB vs The Numbers 85%, TMDB vs Wikidata 90% (within 15%). Worldwide revenue: 81–87%. Domestic gross across The Numbers, Box Office Mojo and RT: 92–97%. Runtime: 92–93% within 5 minutes. MPAA rating: the three sources agree on 99%.
6. **Release dates often don't.** TMDB's date is within 7 days of The Numbers / Box Office Mojo for only 74–75% of films. TMDB often records the first release anywhere (a festival or a foreign market); the others record the US release. Release month is an allowed input, so Phase 3 has to pick one definition.
7. **Matt's domestic-as-worldwide risk is larger than first counted:** 434 films (Matt: 396) have TMDB revenue equal to RT domestic. **The Numbers has a higher worldwide figure for 220 of them**, a direct repair.

**Coverage is uneven** (new)
8. **Every extra source covers big films far better than small ones.** The Numbers matches 36% of $1–5M films vs 88% of $60M+; MPAA and source material 34–35% vs 88%; director 61% vs 88%; franchise 3% vs 42%. Small films are where most losers are, so a missing value is not random. RT stefanoleone992 (scraped in 2020) has actors for only 5% of stress-period films.
9. **Franchise is thin and partly garbled:** 14% coverage; 92 of 1,004 values look like several franchise names run together (e.g. "BatmanDark Knight Trilogy").
10. **Track records are sparse:** 63% of directors and 67% of production companies appear in only one usable film.

**Keys and duplicates**
11. **Duplicates (fixed in the build, 2026-11-23).** The first profile found title+year pairs that were the same film entered twice (*Spider-Man: No Way Home*, *Timber Falls*): the build's rule required runtime within 5 minutes, and one copy had runtime 0. The rule now treats 0 as unknown, which also caught *WALL·E* and *Black Panther: Wakanda Forever*. 3 pairs remain and are **not** duplicates: *Underdogs* (two different 2013 films), *Uncharted 2* (a video game, entered twice) and a junk *Blue Beetle* entry ($400M revenue, runtime 0). Those are cleaning issues. 2 usable films share a Wikidata item.
12. **Review duplicates (fixed in the build).** The stefanoleone992 review file had 120,945 exact duplicate rows and the andrezaza file 12,394 repeated review ids; both are dropped before the rollups.

**Raw-file notes:** The Numbers has 150 release dates after the access date (up to 2068); none reach the usable population. RT sl reviews have 83 placeholder dates (1800-01-01). The Box Office Mojo scraper has no license.

=== md cell 35
### 3k. Proposed dispositions and phase gate (DRAFT, pending Tanner + Matt sign-off)

Matt's §3k rows 1–12 still apply. These are the additions for the unified dataset. **None are applied here.**

| # | Flag | Evidence | Proposed disposition | Treatment | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U1 | Population now multi-source | 6,931 films; 1,168 use The Numbers / Wikidata financials | Requires a contract amendment | Dated amendment: population = 2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0 **from TMDB, The Numbers or Wikidata**, with source precedence stated | Amendment recorded in the contract file |
| U2 | Added films skew to losers | 79% vs 65% losers | Usable; report it | Report results on the full population and on Matt's TMDB-only population as a sensitivity check | Capture on both populations |
| U3 | Domestic-as-worldwide revenue | 434 films; The Numbers higher for 220 | Requires repair | Replace TMDB revenue with The Numbers worldwide where TMDB = RT domestic and The Numbers is higher. Flag the other 214. | Loser rate before / after |
| U4 | Source disagreement on budget / revenue | 81–90% agree within 15% | Requires a rule | Keep precedence TMDB → The Numbers → Wikidata, but hand-check films where they disagree by > 2× | Hand-check sample error rate |
| U5 | Release date definitions differ | 74% agree within 7 days | Requires a rule | Use the US release date (The Numbers / Box Office Mojo) where available, TMDB otherwise; keep the source | Month distribution before / after |
| U6 | Coverage skews by budget | The Numbers 36% vs 88%; director 61% vs 88% | Usable with a limitation | Every optional input gets an "unknown" indicator; no dropped rows | Loser rate by known / unknown |
| U7 | Leftover duplicates | Runtime 0 blocked the merge rule | **Done** (build, 2026-11-23) | Runtime 0 counts as unknown; 4 more films merged | 3 same-title pairs left, none duplicates |
| U8 | Review duplicates | 120,945 + 12,394 duplicate reviews | **Done** (build, 2026-11-23) | Dropped before the rollups | Counts reported in the build |
| U11 | Junk entries | *Uncharted 2* (video game), *Blue Beetle* copy with $400M revenue and runtime 0 | Requires repair | Cleaning rule for runtime-0 TMDB entries that collide with a real film | Pair count after cleaning |
| U9 | Franchise field | 14% coverage, 92 garbled values | Investigate | See `FEATURE_IDEAS.md` (sequel / franchise); likely needs Wikidata series data | Coverage after |
| U10 | Candidate inputs not in the contract | MPAA, source, creative type, writer, cast, franchise | Needs a decision | Decide which to add by amendment before Phase 3 features | Decision recorded |

**Proposed phase gate: CONTINUE**, after U1 (amendment). Build fixes U7 and U8 are done. The S4 readiness verdict still belongs to step 12.

content.text:
I added `film_uid` and the reviews table, and fixed a duplicate problem I found along the way. Everything is committed and pushed to `tanner/data-exploration`.

**New duplicate problem, fixed**
- About 120 films sat in two rows because The Numbers spells titles differently from TMDB: *Star Wars **Ep. VII***, *Kill Bill: **Volume** 1*, *Harry Potter and the **Sorcerer's** Stone*.
- A second, looser matching pass now joins them. Matches need similar titles plus the same year and the same budget or revenue.
- Usable films went from 6,928 to **6,838**. The roughly 90 we lost were counted twice.
- About 10 are still split because the titles share almost nothing (*X-Men 2* vs *X2*, *F9: The Fast Saga* vs *F9*). Fixing those means hand-listing them.

**`film_uid`**
- It's `tmdb-<id>`, or `tn-<The Numbers URL slug>` for films not in TMDB, e.g. `tn-Marvels-The-(2023)`.
- It's the first column and doesn't change between rebuilds.

**Reviews**
- The new `reviews_unified.csv` has one row per review: about 1.48M reviews of 10,475 films, linked by `film_uid`.
- The duplicates we dropped were only exact copies. I checked every column, so every distinct review is kept.
- The films table keeps a review consensus per film: % fresh and review counts from each source, plus RT's Tomatometer and critics-consensus text.

I re-ran your profile notebook, and its numbers now match the rebuilt table.

## Summary
Checkpoint: every source is now assembled into one table with one row per film, and Data Understanding (plan steps 8–9) has been re-run on it.

**Why:** TMDB alone gives 5,766 usable films, because most TMDB rows have no financials. Adding The Numbers and Wikidata financials raises that to **6,838**, and the test set grows from 1,086 to 1,264.

## What's in it
- **`notebooks/00_build_dataset.ipynb`** (team-owned, runs top to bottom) builds:
  - `data/clean/films_unified.csv`: one row per film, keyed by `film_uid` (`tmdb-<id>` / `tn-<The Numbers slug>`). It carries every source column, combined `fin_budget` / `fin_revenue` and a `usable` flag, plus per-film review summaries.
  - `data/clean/reviews_unified.csv`: one row per critic review, keyed by `film_uid`.
  - Both files are gitignored; each person rebuilds them.
- **Sources:** TMDB, The Numbers, a Wikidata snapshot (committed), Box Office Mojo, and both RT movie and review files.
- **Matching:** title + year matching, plus a second, looser pass for The Numbers. Matt's RT join rules are reproduced exactly; his 4,671 of 4,673 pairs are kept. A dedupe step keeps one row per film.
- **Hand-check:** 50 The Numbers matches, 50/50 correct (error ≤ 7.1%, 95% CI upper bound).
- **`notebooks/Edwards-A10.ipynb`:** Matt's §2–§3 re-run on the unified table. It covers the data receipt for the new sources, the profile, source agreement and coverage. Draft dispositions are in 3k (U1–U11).
- **`notebooks/A10-master.ipynb`:** an empty master notebook. The README and `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` describe the workflow: personal notebooks, then promote to the master by PR.
- **`FEATURE_IDEAS.md`:** a running list of feature ideas. First entry: sequel / franchise.

## Needs Matt
- [ ] Review the 3k dispositions, especially **U1**: the population is now multi-source, which needs a contract amendment.
- [ ] Decide which RT reviews upload to cite: priyamchoksi (MIT) or andrezaza (CC0).
- [ ] After merging, run `tools/get_data.py`, then run `00_build_dataset.ipynb`.

## Known open items
- About 10 films are still split across two rows because their titles share almost nothing (*X-Men 2* vs *X2*).
- Cleaning items: junk entries (U11) and domestic-as-worldwide revenue (U3).
EOF

The **budget** has to be at least $1M. Box office only has to be **above $0**, so a film can earn far less than $1M and still count.

message.content: Why?

content.text:
Because budget is known before the film is made, and revenue is the thing we're predicting.

- **Budget ≥ $1M sets the scope.** The screen is for real financing decisions, and micro-budget films are a different business with unreliable data. Budget is known before production, so filtering on it is fair.
- **Revenue has no floor because it's the outcome.** A rule like "revenue ≥ $1M" would remove the films that flopped hardest, which are exactly the money-losers we're trying to catch. The model would learn from a world where big flops don't exist. That's selecting on the outcome.
- **Revenue > 0 is only there because 0 means "unknown."** TMDB writes 0 when it has no box office figure, not when a film earned nothing. Dropping those rows removes films with no label. It doesn't remove bad performers.

The catch is that some tiny revenues are junk, like *Aquajots*: $100M budget, $1 revenue. Those get fixed in cleaning, case by case, not with a blanket floor.

content.text:
Fair challenge. Successes like *Paranormal Activity* and *Napoleon Dynamite* do exist. The data is the problem, not the idea:

| Budget | Films | Have revenue | Loser rate (if revenue known) |
|---|---|---|---|
| < $1K | 12,214 | 14% | 72% |
| $1K–100K | 13,287 | **7%** | 64% |
| $100K–1M | 4,984 | **19%** | 64% |
| $1–5M | 4,190 | 40% | 70% |
| $20M+ | 2,850 | 91% | 63% |

- **Budgets under $1K are mostly junk.** These are typos and placeholders, like "5" meaning $5M.
- **Revenue is mostly missing under $1M.** Only 7–19% of those films have a box office figure. The ones that do are mostly films that got a theatrical release and someone reported the numbers, so they aren't a fair sample. The S4 missing-revenue problem we already have would get much worse.
- **It's a different business.** Micro-budget films mostly make money from festival sales and streaming deals, not box office, so "revenue ≥ 2.5× budget" doesn't describe success the same way.

**Can it change?** Yes, but the $1M floor is in the frozen contract. Changing it needs a dated amendment that you and Matt both agree to.

If you're curious, a middle option is a sensitivity check: run the final model once with a lower floor, like $100K, and see whether results hold. That answers your question without changing the main population.

74 A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md
# A10 Project Purpose Contract — FROZEN 2026-11-17

Date drafted: 2026-11-17. Analyst: Matt Sorensen. AI role: Problem Setter, then Challenger (Claude Code, decision-statement-builder skill).
Source candidate: #1 in `report/A10_problem_scan_2026-11-17.md`.
Status: **FROZEN 2026-11-17, approved by Matt Sorensen.** This was done before any analysis of how inputs relate to the outcome; only structural profiling and join tests have been run. Any later change requires a dated amendment, added below, with a stated reason.

## Contract fields

| Field | Contract answer |
|---|---|
| **Purpose pathway** | **Predictive** (the one primary path). An explanatory layer reports how much director track record adds to the prediction. That's association only, with no causal claim. |
| **Decision** | At the financing stage, before production, the acquisitions team decides for each incoming project whether to **flag for deep review**, **proceed on standard review**, or **pass**. |
| **Action** | Each year, the 20% of projects with the highest predicted risk go to deep review (comparable-film analysis, a second reader, renegotiating terms). The rest get standard review. The screen never rejects a project on its own. |
| **Decision time** | When the financing decision is made, before production. **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, director's track record from earlier films only, production companies' track record from earlier films only, planned runtime, planned release month and quarter, original language, production country. **Prohibited inputs (known only after release):** revenue, box office, vote counts and averages, popularity, critic and audience scores, review text, TMDB keywords (crowd-edited after release). |
| **Population & unit** | Unit = **one feature film at its financing decision.** Population = feature films released 2000–2023 with a reported budget ≥ $1M and reported worldwide revenue > 0, excluding adult titles. Training: 2000–2015. Test: 2016–2019. Stress test: 2020–2023 (COVID era), reported separately. |
| **Outcome / target & horizon** | Positive class = **"money-loser": worldwide revenue < 2.5 × budget.** The 2.5× multiple is a labeled assumption (a commonly cited rule of thumb for covering marketing and the exhibitor's share). It's rerun at 1×, 2× and 3× as a sensitivity check. Horizon = full theatrical run as recorded in TMDB. The model estimates each project's probability of being a money-loser. |
| **Baseline** | (a) **Random 20% flagging**, which catches losers at the base rate (the floor). (b) **A simple rule:** flag projects in the genre × budget-tier groups with the highest historical loss rate, using training years only. The model has to beat (b), not just (a). |
| **Evidence standard** | On the 2016–2019 test films, the share of all money-losers that fall inside the flagged top 20% (capture rate). The model must beat rule (b) by **≥ 5 percentage points**, with a bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. Also report precision at 20%, calibration, and the result for the 2020–2023 stress set. *Bar confirmed by Matt at the freeze.* |
| **Value** | More money-losers reach deep review without adding review workload: same 20% capacity, better targeting. No written reasoning exists for most of these. The contract and `PLAN.md` state the choices, not why they were made.

| Choice | Where it came from | My take |
|---|---|---|
| **2000–2023** | Not documented. My guess: TMDB financials get thin before 2000, and films after 2023 hadn't finished their theatrical run when the data was pulled. | The end date is defensible. The start date is arbitrary and could be revisited. |
| **$1M budget floor** | "Confirmed by Matt." The reason given is that micro-budget films are out of scope. | Your version is reasonable: a $100K floor, with anything under $1K treated as a cleaning issue. One caveat: under $1M, only 7–19% of films have a revenue figure. |
| **2.5× = money-loser** | Industry rule of thumb. The theater keeps about half the box office, and marketing often costs about as much as production, so a film needs roughly 2–2.5× its budget to break even. | Reasonable, but it's a heuristic, not something the data showed. The plan already reruns it at 1×, 2× and 3×. |
| **Narrow input list** | Matt's rule: only what's known before production. | Partly agree. MPAA rating, source material, cast, writer, distributor and franchise are known at financing and should be added. Options: keep it as a separate check (current), add a COVID-era indicator, or test on 2022–23 once theaters recovered. Whatever we pick, training has to stay earlier than testing. |

**Suggested next step:** I draft one amendment proposal with your positions and the reasoning. You and Matt go through it together, and only what you both agree on gets added to the contract.

import pandas as pd
f = pd.read_csv("data/clean/films_unified.csv", usecols=["year","fin_budget","fin_revenue"], low_memory=False)
f = f[f.year.between(2000,2023)]
for floor in [1e6, 1e5]:
    u = f[f.fin_budget.ge(floor) & f.fin_revenue.gt(0)]
    lab = u.fin_revenue < 2.5*u.fin_budget
    sp = pd.cut(u.year,[1999,2015,2019,2023],labels=["train","test","stress"]).value_counts().sort_index().to_dict()
    print(f"floor ${floor:,.0f}: {len(u):,} films, losers {lab.mean():.1%}, {sp}")
b = f[f.fin_budget.between(1e5,1e6,inclusive="left") & f.fin_revenue.gt(0)]
m = b.fin_revenue/b.fin_budget
print(f"$100K-1M films: {len(b)}, median multiple {m.median():.2f}, share >= 10x {(m>=10).mean():.0%}")
a = f[f.fin_budget.ge(1e6) & f.fin_revenue.gt(0)]; m2=a.fin_revenue/a.fin_budget
print(f">= $1M films: median multiple {m2.median():.2f}, share >= 10x {(m2>=10).mean():.0%}")
EOF

# A10 Purpose Contract: proposed amendments (DRAFT)

Proposed by Tanner Edwards, 2026-11-23. **Not in effect.** These are changes to `A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md`, which was frozen by Matt alone. Each one takes effect only when Tanner and Matt both agree. Agreed items are then copied into the contract's **Amendments** section with the date and reason.

| # | Contract field | Current | Proposed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Population: years | 2000–2023, no reason stated | **Keep 2000–2023**, and record the reason | Proposed |
| A2 | Population: budget floor | Budget ≥ $1M | **Budget ≥ $100K**. Budgets under $1K are data errors and are handled in cleaning. | Proposed |
| A3 | Outcome: 2.5× multiple | "Commonly cited rule of thumb" | **Keep 2.5×**, labeled as an industry convention, not a data finding | Proposed |
| A4 | Allowed inputs | Fixed list of 8 | **Re-open after cleaning.** Add every input known at the financing decision. | Open: list to follow |
| A5 | 2020–2023 stress test | COVID years reported separately | Not discussed yet | Open |

## A1. Keep 2000–2023, with a reason
**Reason:** 24 years of films is enough to be relevant to today's market. Before 2000, the data gets thin, and dollar amounts would need inflation adjustment to compare fairly. The end year stays at 2023 because later films hadn't finished their theatrical run when the data was pulled.

## A2. Lower the budget floor to $100K
**Reason:** Low-budget films are part of the financing decision, and they're where the biggest margins happen. Among usable films with a $100K–$1M budget, 14% returned 10× their budget or more, against 4% of films above $1M. Leaving them out hides the upside the screen should help find.

**Effect** (`films_unified.csv`, 2026-11-23):

| | $1M floor | $100K floor |
|---|---|---|
| Usable films | 6,838 | 7,671 |
| Train / test / stress | 4,952 / 1,264 / 622 | 5,554 / 1,426 / 691 |
| Money-losers at 2.5× | 67.5% | 66.9% |

**Watch:** Under $1M, only 7–19% of films with a budget also have a revenue figure. The films that do may lean toward ones that got a theatrical release and reported their numbers. The S4 check (films with a budget but no revenue) has to be rerun on the new population.

**Also changes:** prohibited use #4 ("doesn't cover micro-budget films (< $1M)") becomes "< $100K". `BUDGET_FLOOR` in `00_build_dataset.ipynb` changes to 100,000.

## A3. Label 2.5× as an industry convention
**Reason:** 2.5× is a rule of thumb, not something the data shows. Theaters keep roughly half the box office, and marketing often costs about as much as production, so a film needs about 2–2.5× its budget to break even. The report must say that the threshold is an industry convention, cite a source for it, and show the 1×, 2× and 3× sensitivity results next to it.

## A4. Inputs: re-open the allowed list (pending)
The frozen list allows 8 inputs. The rule behind it stays: **only information known at the financing decision, before production.** The list itself is re-opened. After cleaning, every column that meets the rule is proposed here with its evidence. Candidates so far: MPAA rating, source material, creative type, production method, writer, cast, distributor, franchise / sequel (see `FEATURE_IDEAS.md`).

## A5. COVID-era stress test (not discussed yet)

.venv/bin/python - <<'EOF'
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
f = pd.read_csv("data/clean/films_unified.csv", low_memory=False)
f = f[f.year.between(2000,2023)]
dom = f[["rt_boxOffice_usd","bom_domestic_gross","tn_Domestic Gross (USD)"]].where(lambda d: d>0).bfill(axis=1).iloc[:,0]
f["dom"]=dom
f["period"]=pd.cut(f.year,[1999,2015,2019,2023],labels=["train","test","stress"])
for lo,hi,name in [(1e6,np.inf,"$1M+ (current)"),(1e5,np.inf,"$100K+ (proposed)"),(1e5,1e6,"$100K-1M only")]:
    b=f[f.fin_budget.ge(lo)&f.fin_budget.lt(hi)]
    has=b.fin_revenue.gt(0)
    print(f"\n== {name}: {len(b):,} films with budget; {1-has.mean():.1%} missing revenue")
    print("   missing by period:", b.groupby("period",observed=True).apply(lambda d:1-d.fin_revenue.gt(0).mean()).round(3).to_dict())
    miss=b[~has]
    print(f"   of missing: {miss.dom.notna().mean():.1%} have a domestic box office figure")
    # cross-check: domestic multiple, films with vs without worldwide revenue
    w=b[has & b.dom.notna()]; m=miss[miss.dom.notna()]
    print(f"   domestic/budget median: with revenue {(w.dom/w.fin_budget).median():.2f} (n={len(w)}), missing revenue {(m.dom/m.fin_budget).median():.2f} (n={len(m)})")
    print(f"   domestic < 1x budget: with revenue {((w.dom/w.fin_budget)<1).mean():.0%}, missing revenue {((m.dom/m.fin_budget)<1).mean():.0%}")
EOF

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
f = pd.read_csv("data/clean/films_unified.csv", low_memory=False)
f = f[f.year.between(2000,2023)]
dom = f[["rt_boxOffice_usd","bom_domestic_gross","tn_Domestic Gross (USD)"]].where(lambda d: d>0).bfill(axis=1).iloc[:,0]
f["dom"]=dom
f["period"]=pd.cut(f.year,[1999,2015,2019,2023],labels=["train","test","stress"])
for lo,hi,name in [(1e6,np.inf,"$1M+ (current)"),(1e5,np.inf,"$100K+ (proposed)"),(1e5,1e6,"$100K-1M only")]:
    b=f[f.fin_budget.ge(lo)&f.fin_budget.lt(hi)]
    has=b.fin_revenue.gt(0)
    print(f"\n== {name}: {len(b):,} films with budget; {1-has.mean():.1%} missing revenue")
    print("   missing by period:", b.groupby("period",observed=True).apply(lambda d:1-d.fin_revenue.gt(0).mean()).round(3).to_dict())
    miss=b[~has]
    print(f"   of missing: {miss.dom.notna().mean():.1%} have a domestic box office figure")
    # cross-check: domestic multiple, films with vs without worldwide revenue
    w=b[has & b.dom.notna()]; m=miss[miss.dom.notna()]

# A10 Purpose Contract: proposed amendments (DRAFT)

Proposed by Tanner Edwards, 2026-11-23. **Not in effect.** These are changes to `A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md`, which was frozen by Matt alone. Each one takes effect only when Tanner and Matt both agree. Agreed items are then copied into the contract's **Amendments** section with the date and reason.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Population: years | 2000–2023, no reason stated | **Keep 2000–2023**, and record the reason | Proposed |
| A2 | Population: budget floor | Budget ≥ $1M | **Budget ≥ $100K**. Budgets under $1K are data errors and are handled in cleaning. | Proposed |
| A3 | Outcome: 2.5× multiple | "Commonly cited rule of thumb" | **Keep 2.5×**, labeled as an industry convention, not a data finding | Proposed |

## A1. Keep 2000–2023, with a reason
**Reason:** 24 years of films is enough to be relevant to today's market. Before 2000, the data gets thin, and dollar amounts would need inflation adjustment to compare fairly. The end year stays at 2023 because later films hadn't finished their theatrical run when the data was pulled.

## A2. Lower the budget floor to $100K
**Reason:** Low-budget films are part of the financing decision, and they're where the biggest margins happen. Among usable films with a $100K–$1M budget, 14% returned 10× their budget or more, against 4% of films above $1M. Leaving them out hides the upside the screen should help find.

**Effect** (`films_unified.csv`, 2026-11-23):

| | $1M floor | $100K floor |
|---|---|---|
| Usable films | 6,838 | 7,671 |
| Train / test / stress | 4,952 / 1,264 / 622 | 5,554 / 1,426 / 691 |
| Money-losers at 2.5× | 67.5% | 66.9% |

**Watch:** Under $1M, only 7–19% of films with a budget also have a revenue figure. The films that do may lean toward ones that got a theatrical release and reported their numbers. The S4 check (films with a budget but no revenue) has to be rerun on the new population.

**Also changes:** prohibited use #4 ("doesn't cover micro-budget films (< $1M)") becomes "< $100K". `BUDGET_FLOOR` in `00_build_dataset.ipynb` changes to 100,000.

## A3. Label 2.5× as an industry convention
**Reason:** 2.5× is a rule of thumb, not something the data shows. Theaters keep roughly half the box office, and marketing often costs about as much as production, so a film needs about 2–2.5× its budget to break even. The report must say that the threshold is an industry convention, cite a source for it, and show the 1×, 2× and 3× sensitivity results next to it.

## A4. Inputs: re-open the allowed list (pending)
The frozen list allows 8 inputs. The rule behind it stays: **only information known at the financing decision, before production.** The list itself is re-opened. After cleaning, every column that meets the rule is proposed here with its evidence. Candidates so far: MPAA rating, source material, creative type, production method, writer, cast, distributor, franchise / sequel (see `FEATURE_IDEAS.md`).

## A5. COVID-era stress test (not discussed yet)

I added §4 to your notebook. It covers 50 repeated columns grouped into 19 concepts, measured on the 6,838 usable films.

**Combining helps a lot**

| Concept | Best single source | All sources combined |
|---|---|---|
| Budget / revenue | 87–88% | 100% (already combined in `fin_*`) |
| MPAA rating | 64% | **76%** |
| Domestic gross | 64% | 76% (post-release, only used for checks) |

**Combining barely helps; one column already covers almost everything**

| Concept | Main column fills | Other sources add | Extra columns |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime | 98% | +0% | 3 columns add 1–26 films each |
| Release date | 98% | +2% | 3 columns add **0** films |
| Genre | 97% | +2% | `sl_genres` adds 0 |
| Language | 98% | +2% | |
| Country | 95% | +3% | |
| Director | 80% | +2% | |
| Writer | 78% | +3% | |
| Critic score | 76% | +3% | 2 of the 4 columns add 0 |

- Cast: 60%.
- Franchise: 15%.
- Source material and creative type: about 63%. Only The Numbers has them.
- Director is missing everywhere for 1,209 films (18%).

- Release date: TMDB records the first release anywhere; the others record the US release.
- Genre: each source uses a different list of genres.

import nbformat
nb = nbformat.v4.new_notebook()
nb.metadata["kernelspec"] = {"name": "emba560-a10", "display_name": "Python (EMBA 560 A10)", "language": "python"}
M = nbformat.v4.new_markdown_cell; C = nbformat.v4.new_code_cell
cells = []
cells.append(M("""# 01 · Clean the unified dataset

**Shared pipeline notebook (team-owned).** Run it after `00_build_dataset.ipynb`. Changes go through a PR.

**Input:** `data/clean/films_unified.csv` (one row per film, every source's columns side by side).
**Outputs** (gitignored; rebuilt on every run):
- `data/clean/films_clean.csv`: same films and rows, plus one **combined column per fact** (runtime, US release date, rating, genre…), with a `_src` column showing which source supplied the value and a `_missing` flag for inputs that aren't always filled.
- `data/clean/films_clean_columns.csv`: a dictionary giving every column's group and role.

**Why:** each fact (runtime, genre, rating…) comes from several sources, each in its own column. The rules, agreed in `Edwards-A10.ipynb` §4b (Tanner, 2026-11-24), are:
1. Each fact gets **one combined column**, filled from the fullest source first, then from the others in a fixed order.
2. Only real values count. TMDB's `0` for budget, revenue or runtime means unknown, and so does Box Office Mojo's `-` distributor.
3. Values are put into one format before combining (rating codes, genre names, language codes, country names).
4. The original source columns are **kept but grouped as `source detail`**: there for audits, never model inputs.
5. Inputs that aren't always filled get a `_missing` flag. Blanks aren't guessed or dropped, because coverage depends on budget (Data Understanding §3h).

**This notebook never removes films.** Later cleaning steps (U3 revenue repair, U11 junk entries, standardizing company names) will be added here as numbered sections."""))
cells.append(M("## 1. Setup"))
cells.append(C('''from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 60)
pd.set_option("display.width", 200)

CLEAN = Path("../data/clean")
films = pd.read_csv(CLEAN / "films_unified.csv", low_memory=False)
assert films["film_uid"].is_unique
n_rows = len(films)
usable = films["usable"]
print(f"films_unified.csv: {n_rows:,} films x {films.shape[1]} columns ({usable.sum():,} usable)")'''))
cells.append(M("""## 2. Helpers

- `real(col)`: the column with placeholder values turned into blanks.
- `combine(name, [cols])`: the first real value across the columns, in order, plus `<name>_src` naming the source column it came from."""))
cells.append(C('''ZERO_MISSING = {"budget", "revenue", "runtime", "tn_Domestic Gross (USD)"}   # 0 = unknown in these sources
DASH_MISSING = {"bom_distributor"}


def real(c):
    s = films[c]
    if c in ZERO_MISSING:
        s = s.where(s.ne(0))
    if s.dtype == object or str(s.dtype) == "str":
        s = s.where(s.astype(str).str.strip().ne(""))
    if c in DASH_MISSING:
        s = s.where(s.astype(str).str.strip().ne("-"))
    return s


def combine(name, cols, values=None):
    """First real value across `cols` (in order). `values` optionally supplies already-formatted Series per col."""
    vals = pd.concat([(values or {}).get(c, real(c)).rename(c) for c in cols], axis=1)
    src = pd.Series(pd.NA, index=films.index, dtype="string")
    for c in reversed(cols):
        src = src.mask(vals[c].notna(), c)
    films[name] = vals.bfill(axis=1).iloc[:, 0].infer_objects() if len(cols) > 1 else vals.iloc[:, 0]
    films[name + "_src"] = src
    u = films.loc[usable, name]
    print(f"{name:<22} usable films filled {u.notna().mean():6.1%}   by source: "
          + ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.0%}" for k, v in films.loc[usable, name + '_src'].value_counts(normalize=True).items()))


def split_list(s, sep=","):
    return s.fillna("").astype(str).map(lambda x: [t.strip() for t in x.split(sep) if t.strip()])


def join_list(lists):
    return lists.map(lambda l: ", ".join(dict.fromkeys(l)) if l else np.nan)'''))
cells.append(M("""## 3. Money (C1–C3)

`fin_budget` and `fin_revenue` are already combined by the build (TMDB → The Numbers → Wikidata) and are kept unchanged. `domestic_gross` is new: The Numbers → Box Office Mojo → RT. It's post-release, so it's **for checks only** (S4, U3), never an input. A The Numbers domestic gross of 0 counts as unknown."""))
cells.append(C('''combine("domestic_gross", ["tn_Domestic Gross (USD)", "bom_domestic_gross", "rt_boxOffice_usd"])'''))
cells.append(M("""## 4. Runtime and release date (C4–C6)

- `runtime_min`: TMDB → RT → The Numbers → RT sl (sources agree on 92–93% of films within 5 minutes).
- `release_date_us`: **the US theatrical date** (decision, Tanner 2026-11-24): The Numbers → RT theatrical → Box Office Mojo first day.
- `release_date`: US date where known, otherwise TMDB's (first release anywhere). `release_date_src` records which. `release_month` and `release_quarter` come from it.
- `year` (TMDB) is **not changed**: the population and the train/test split stay as the contract defines them."""))
cells.append(C('''combine("runtime_min", ["runtime", "rt_runtimeMinutes", "tn_Running Time (minutes)", "sl_runtime"])

dates = {c: pd.to_datetime(films[c], errors="coerce") for c in
         ["tn_Release Date", "rt_releaseDateTheaters", "bom_first_date", "release_date"]}
combine("release_date_us", ["tn_Release Date", "rt_releaseDateTheaters", "bom_first_date"], dates)
dates["release_date_us"] = films["release_date_us"]
films["release_date_tmdb"] = dates["release_date"]
combine("release_date", ["release_date_us", "release_date"], {"release_date_us": dates["release_date_us"], "release_date": dates["release_date"]})
films["release_date_src"] = films["release_date_src"].replace({"release_date_us": "us", "release_date": "tmdb_first_release"})
films["release_month"] = films["release_date"].dt.month
films["release_quarter"] = films["release_date"].dt.quarter
films = films.drop(columns="release_date_us_src")'''))
cells.append(M("""## 5. Genre (C7)

TMDB genres (19 categories) first. RT and The Numbers genres fill only TMDB's blanks, translated to TMDB's names. Genres with no TMDB equivalent (*Biography*, *Sports*, *Holiday*, *LGBTQ+*, *Multiple Genres*) are left out of the fill."""))
cells.append(C('''RT_GENRE = {"Action": "Action", "Adventure": "Adventure", "Animation": "Animation", "Anime": "Animation",
            "Comedy": "Comedy", "Stand-up": "Comedy", "Crime": "Crime", "Documentary": "Documentary", "Drama": "Drama",
            "Fantasy": "Fantasy", "History": "History", "Horror": "Horror", "Kids & family": "Family",
            "Music": "Music", "Musical": "Music", "Mystery & thriller": ["Mystery", "Thriller"], "Romance": "Romance",
            "Sci-fi": "Science Fiction", "War": "War", "Western": "Western"}
TN_GENRE = {"Action": "Action", "Adventure": "Adventure", "Black Comedy": "Comedy", "Comedy": "Comedy",
            "Concert/Performance": "Music", "Documentary": "Documentary", "Drama": "Drama", "Horror": "Horror",
            "Musical": "Music", "Reality": "Documentary", "Romantic Comedy": ["Romance", "Comedy"],
            "Thriller/Suspense": "Thriller", "Western": "Western"}


def translate(s, mapping):
    def one(lst):
        out = []
        for g in lst:
            m = mapping.get(g)
            out += m if isinstance(m, list) else ([m] if m else [])
        return out
    return join_list(split_list(s).map(one))


combine("genres_all", ["genres", "rt_genre", "tn_Genre"],
        {"genres": real("genres"), "rt_genre": translate(films["rt_genre"], RT_GENRE),
         "tn_Genre": translate(films["tn_Genre"].astype("string").str.strip(), TN_GENRE)})
TMDB_GENRES = set(g for l in split_list(films["genres"]) for g in l)
assert set(g for l in split_list(films["genres_all"]) for g in l) <= TMDB_GENRES'''))
cells.append(M("""## 6. MPAA rating (C8)

The Numbers → RT → RT sl, standardized to **G / PG / PG-13 / R / NC-17 / NR** (sources agree on 99% of films). The Numbers' run-on text ("NC-17for explicit sexual content…") is cut to its leading rating; "Not Rated" and "NR" become NR; TV ratings and "Open" count as missing.

⚠️ RT never uses NR, so a blank RT rating can mean "never rated". `mpaa_rating` NR and missing are kept separate."""))
cells.append(C('''def std_rating(s):
    s = s.astype("string").str.strip()
    m = s.str.extract(r"^(NC-?17|PG-13|PG|G|R|Not Rated|NR|Unrated)", expand=False)
    return m.replace({"NC17": "NC-17", "Not Rated": "NR", "Unrated": "NR"})


combine("mpaa_rating", ["tn_MPAA Rating", "rt_rating", "sl_content_rating"],
        {c: std_rating(films[c]) for c in ["tn_MPAA Rating", "rt_rating", "sl_content_rating"]})
films.loc[usable, "mpaa_rating"].value_counts(dropna=False)'''))
cells.append(M("""## 7. People and companies (C9–C13)

Fill only: the second source fills the first source's blanks, with no name matching yet.
- `director`, `writer`: RT → RT sl. They're used as **track records from earlier films only**.
- `production_companies`: TMDB → The Numbers → RT sl.
- `distributor`: RT → Box Office Mojo.

**Cast (C11) is dropped as an input** (Tanner, 2026-11-24): only 5% coverage in 2020–23. `sl_actors` stays in source detail.

Company and distributor names differ by source ("Warner Bros." vs "Warner Bros. Pictures"). Standardizing them is a later cleaning step."""))
cells.append(C('''combine("director", ["rt_director", "sl_directors"])
combine("writer", ["rt_writer", "sl_authors"])
combine("production_companies", ["production_companies", "tn_Production/Financing Companies", "sl_production_company"],
        {"production_companies": real("production_companies"),
         "tn_Production/Financing Companies": join_list(split_list(films["tn_Production/Financing Companies"])),
         "sl_production_company": real("sl_production_company")})
films = films.rename(columns={"production_companies_src": "production_companies_src"})
combine("distributor", ["rt_distributor", "bom_distributor"])'''))
cells.append(M("""## 8. Country and language (C14–C15)

- `countries`: TMDB → The Numbers, with The Numbers' names translated to TMDB's ("United States" → "United States of America"). The Numbers writes Taiwan as "Taiwan, Province of China", which splits on the comma; the "Province of China" fragment is dropped.
- `original_language`: TMDB (ISO code) → RT (language name → code). `tn_Languages` lists every spoken language, not the original one, so it stays in source detail."""))
cells.append(C('''TN_COUNTRY = {"United States": "United States of America", "Republic of Korea": "South Korea",
              "Russian Federation": "Russia", "Islamic Republic of Iran": "Iran",
              "Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela": "Venezuela", "Province of China": None}
tn_c = join_list(split_list(films["tn_Production Countries"]).map(
    lambda l: [TN_COUNTRY.get(c, c) for c in l if TN_COUNTRY.get(c, c)]))
combine("countries", ["production_countries", "tn_Production Countries"],
        {"production_countries": real("production_countries"), "tn_Production Countries": tn_c})

LANG = {"English": "en", "Hindi": "hi", "French": "fr", "Chinese": "zh", "Korean": "ko", "Spanish": "es",
        "Russian": "ru", "Japanese": "ja", "German": "de", "Italian": "it", "Arabic": "ar", "Norwegian": "no",
        "Tamil": "ta", "Danish": "da", "Telugu": "te", "Portuguese": "pt", "Turkish": "tr", "Polish": "pl",
        "Finnish": "fi", "Swedish": "sv", "Dutch": "nl", "Malayalam": "ml", "Hebrew": "he", "Romanian": "ro",
        "Czech": "cs", "Thai": "th", "Urdu": "ur", "Indonesian": "id", "Persian": "fa", "Malay": "ms",
        "Latin": "la", "Hungarian": "hu", "Afrikaans": "af", "Cantonese": "cn", "Greek": "el", "Icelandic": "is",
        "Vietnamese": "vi", "Bengali": "bn", "Kannada": "kn", "Marathi": "mr", "Punjabi": "pa", "Tagalog": "tl",
        "Ukrainian": "uk", "Serbian": "sr", "Croatian": "hr", "Estonian": "et", "Lithuanian": "lt", "Slovak": "sk"}
rt_lang = films["rt_originalLanguage"].astype("string").str.replace(r"\\s*\\(.*\\)", "", regex=True).str.strip().map(LANG)
combine("original_language", ["original_language", "rt_originalLanguage"],
        {"original_language": real("original_language"), "rt_originalLanguage": rt_lang})'''))
cells.append(M("""## 9. Review consensus and audience score (C16–C17): description only

Both are **post-release**, so they're never model inputs. They're kept to describe films and to show how reception relates to money-losers (Tanner, 2026-11-24).
- `critic_pct_fresh` (0–100): RT reviews % fresh → RT Tomatometer → RT sl Tomatometer.
- `audience_score` (0–100): TMDB average vote × 10 (only when the film has votes) → RT audience → RT sl audience."""))
cells.append(C('''combine("critic_pct_fresh", ["rtrev_pct_fresh", "rt_tomatoMeter", "sl_tomatometer_rating"])

cells.append(M("""## 10. Franchise, source material, creative type (C18)

    for i, p in enumerate(PROTECT):

films["source_material"] = real("tn_Source")
films["creative_type"] = real("tn_Creative Type")

# emba-560-data-analytics

EMBA 560 **A10** team project: a pre-production **money-loser screen** for film financing.
Due **Fri Dec 4, 2026, 3:30 PM**.

- Frozen scope: [`A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md`](A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md)
- Plan, status and session handoff: [`PLAN.md`](PLAN.md)

## Setup (once per machine)

Requires Python 3.12. [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is recommended, but plain `venv` + `pip` works too.

```bash
# 1. Environment
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv -r requirements.txt
#   Windows without uv:  py -3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv\Scripts\pip install -r requirements.txt

# 2. Strip notebook outputs on commit (git filter config is local; each person must run this)
.venv/bin/nbstripout --install          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\nbstripout --install

# 3. Download raw data from Kaggle into data/raw/ (about 1.3 GB, gitignored)
.venv/bin/python tools/get_data.py      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\python tools\get_data.py

# 4. Build the unified dataset: run notebooks/00_build_dataset.ipynb top to bottom
#    -> data/clean/films_unified.csv and data/clean/reviews_unified.csv (gitignored)
```

Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy (e.g. Zscaler), `get_data.py` uses `truststore` so Python trusts the OS certificate store.

## Folder layout

| Folder | Contents | In git? |
|---|---|---|
| `data/raw/` | Kaggle downloads. **Read-only, never edit.** | No (too large) |
| `data/clean/` | Cleaned and derived datasets written by notebooks | Small files only |
| `notebooks/` | Analysis notebooks (outputs stripped on commit) | Yes |
| `tools/` | Helper scripts (`get_data.py`, transcript export) | Yes |
| `ai_logs/` | Unedited AI session transcripts (required in the final zip) | Yes |
| `report/` | Problem scan, contract drafts, Data Receipt, final report | Yes |

Licenses, access dates and grain are recorded in the Data Receipt (`report/`, plan step 8).

## Notebook workflow

**Rules for everyone, including AI assistants working in this repo:**

0. **Data comes from one place.** `notebooks/00_build_dataset.ipynb` merges all sources into `data/clean/films_unified.csv` (one row per film). Every other notebook starts by reading that file and never re-merges raw data. Rerun `00_build_dataset.ipynb` after pulling changes to it. It's team-owned: changes go through a PR.
1. **Personal notebooks are for exploration.** Each person works in their own `notebooks/<LastName>-A10.ipynb` (e.g. `Sorensen-A10.ipynb`, `Edwards-A10.ipynb`). Only the owner edits it.
2. **`notebooks/A10-master.ipynb` is the team's final notebook.** It's what gets submitted. Only work that is solid (verified, runs top to bottom, agreed by both members) moves into it.
3. **Promoting work to the master:** copy the finished cells from your personal notebook into the matching section of the master, make them run standalone (no dependence on the personal notebook's state), Run All, then open a PR. The other member reviews before merging.
4. **Never edit someone else's personal notebook,** and never write exploratory or half-finished work into the master.
5. **Notebook outputs are stripped on commit** (`nbstripout`). Run `nbstripout --install` once after cloning (see Setup).

## Standing rules
- `data/raw/` is never modified. All cleaning happens in notebooks and writes to `data/clean/`.
- The purpose contract is frozen. Changes need a dated amendment with a reason.
- No post-release inputs in the model (revenue, votes, popularity, scores, reviews, keywords).
- Export every AI session to `ai_logs/`.

| `notebooks/Sorensen-A10.ipynb` | Main analysis notebook. §2: Data Receipt and physical checks. §3: univariate profile of all 51 fields, flag register, approved dispositions. §4: TMDB–RT join and its verification | Matt |
| `data/clean/tmdb_rt_crosswalk.csv` | TMDB id ↔ RT id, 4,673 one-to-one pairs with match rule and year/runtime differences. Rebuilt by notebook §4 on every run (not in git) | Matt |
| `data/clean/join_handcheck.csv` | 60 matched pairs (random 50 + 10 rule-2b) hand-checked by Matt, 2026-11-19: all correct. Written once by §4; never overwritten. Force-added to git because it can't be regenerated | Matt |

| `data/clean/edwards_tn_handcheck.csv` | 50 The Numbers ↔ TMDB matches (25 risky) for hand-checking. Written once, never overwritten | Tanner |
| `tools/get_data.py` | Downloads all raw datasets (Kaggle + Box Office Mojo) into `data/raw/` | Tanner |

Cleaning comes first because it changes which films count as losers. Building features on uncleaned labels would mean redoing them.

content.text:
I wrote the deep dive into your notebook as **§6**, with charts and tables for all six columns and a findings summary (6g). I also fixed both of your points:

- **IDs and other logistics:** §5 now lists only the **16** columns that could go into a model. The ids stay in the file for joins but are hidden.
- **Release dates:** `release_date` is now the only date input. Its two ingredients (`_us` and `_tmdb`) moved to source detail.

**What the six columns show**

1. **Runtime turned up junk entries.** The longest "films" are TV series and video games listed at 999 minutes (*God of War*, *The Bear*, *What If...?*). The shortest include a 1-minute Oscars clip with a "$30M" budget. These aren't feature films, so they need cleaning out. A real film's median runtime is 105 minutes.
2. **Genre is good as is.** It's 99.5% filled, with 2–3 genres per film; Drama and Comedy lead.
3. **Production companies:** two-thirds appear in only one film, and the same studio shows up under many names (several "Warner Bros. …" variants). Track records will be thin unless we standardize names or group them into major vs independent.
4. **Distributor:** 77 distributors cover 91% of the films that list one, but the names are messy ("Fox" vs "20th Century Fox"). Grouping into major / mini-major / independent looks more useful than individual names.
5. **Countries:** 65% of films include the US. A few flags (US, UK, France, India, co-production) would capture most of it; 108 separate countries is too many.
6. **Creative type** is useful, but 64% of $1–5M films are blank vs 9% of $60M+ films. It needs its missing flag. I also fixed one stray value that had a tab character in front of it.

Nothing is committed yet. The junk-entry cleanup from finding 1 is the most urgent next step, because those films change both the population and the label.

# A10 Purpose Contract: proposed amendments (DRAFT)

Proposed by Tanner Edwards, 2026-11-23. **Not in effect.** These are changes to `A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md`, which was frozen by Matt alone. Each one takes effect only when Tanner and Matt both agree. Agreed items are then copied into the contract's **Amendments** section with the date and reason.

| # | Contract field | Current | Proposed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Population: years | 2000–2023, no reason stated | **Keep 2000–2023**, and record the reason | Proposed |
| A2 | Population: budget floor | Budget ≥ $1M, no sensitivity check | **Keep $1M for the main analysis; rerun at $100K as a sensitivity check.** Budgets under $1K are data errors and are handled in cleaning. | Proposed |
| A3 | Outcome: 2.5× multiple | "Commonly cited rule of thumb" | **Keep 2.5×**, labeled as an industry convention, not a data finding | Proposed |
| A4 | Allowed inputs | Fixed list of 8 | **Re-open after cleaning.** Add every input known at the financing decision. | Open: list to follow |
| A5 | 2020–2023 stress test | COVID years reported separately | Not discussed yet | Open |

## A1. Keep 2000–2023, with a reason
**Reason:** 24 years of films is enough to be relevant to today's market. Before 2000, the data gets thin, and dollar amounts would need inflation adjustment to compare fairly. The end year stays at 2023 because later films hadn't finished their theatrical run when the data was pulled.

## A2. Keep the $1M floor; add a $100K sensitivity check
**Reason to look below $1M:** Low-budget films are part of the financing decision, and they're where the biggest margins happen. Among usable films with a $100K–$1M budget, 14% returned 10× their budget or more, against 4% of films above $1M.

**Reason not to make it the main population:** the S4 rerun (2026-11-23). Revenue is missing far more often below $1M, and the films that are missing it are mostly losers. So the $100K–$1M films we can see lean toward the winners, which probably inflates the 14% figure too.

| Films with a budget | $1M floor | $100K floor | $100K–1M only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Films | 11,212 | 16,065 | 4,853 |
| Missing revenue | 39% | 52% | 83% |
| Missing revenue, 2020–23 | 52% | 69% | 92% |
| Missing-revenue films with US gross < budget* | 98% | 97% | 93% |

\*Among the 3–5% of missing-revenue films that have a US box office figure.

**Proposal:** the main analysis keeps the $1M floor. The final model is rerun on the $100K population (7,671 usable films: train 5,554 / test 1,426 / stress 691; 66.9% losers), and the report shows both results side by side. Any $100K result is limited to "films with reported revenue."

**Also changes:** the plan adds a step for the $100K sensitivity rerun. `00_build_dataset.ipynb` gets a flag for the $100K population (e.g. `usable_100k`) alongside `usable`.

## A3. Label 2.5× as an industry convention
**Reason:** 2.5× is a rule of thumb, not something the data shows. Theaters keep roughly half the box office, and marketing often costs about as much as production, so a film needs about 2–2.5× its budget to break even. The report must say that the threshold is an industry convention, cite a source for it, and show the 1×, 2× and 3× sensitivity results next to it.

## A4. Inputs: re-open the allowed list (pending)
The frozen list allows 8 inputs. The rule behind it stays: **only information known at the financing decision, before production.** The list itself is re-opened. After cleaning, every column that meets the rule is proposed here with its evidence. Candidates so far: MPAA rating, source material, creative type, production method, writer, cast, distributor, franchise / sequel (see `FEATURE_IDEAS.md`).

## A5. COVID-era stress test (not discussed yet)

9	| A3 | Outcome: 2.5× multiple | "Commonly cited rule of thumb" | **Keep 2.5×**, labeled as an industry convention, not a data finding | Proposed |
10	| A4 | Allowed inputs | Fixed list of 8 | **Re-open after cleaning.** Add every input known at the financing decision. | Open: list to follow |
11	| A5 | 2020–2023 stress test | COVID years reported separately | Not discussed yet | Open |
12	
13	## A1. Keep 2000–2023, with a reason
14	**Reason:** 24 years of films is enough to be relevant to today's market. Before 2000, the data gets thin, and dollar amounts would need inflation adjustment to compare fairly. The end year stays at 2023 because later films hadn't finished their theatrical run when the data was pulled.
15	
16	## A2. Keep the $1M floor; add a $100K sensitivity check
17	**Reason to look below $1M:** Low-budget films are part of the financing decision, and they're where the biggest margins happen. Among usable films with a $100K–$1M budget, 14% returned 10× their budget or more, against 4% of films above $1M.
18	
19	**Reason not to make it the main population:** the S4 rerun (2026-11-23). Revenue is missing far more often below $1M, and the films that are missing it are mostly losers. So the $100K–$1M films we can see lean toward the winners, which probably inflates the 14% figure too.
20	
21	| Films with a budget | $1M floor | $100K floor | $100K–1M only |
22	|---|---|---|---|
23	| Films | 11,212 | 16,065 | 4,853 |
24	| Missing revenue | 39% | 52% | 83% |
25	| Missing revenue, 2020–23 | 52% | 69% | 92% |
26	| Missing-revenue films with US gross < budget* | 98% | 97% | 93% |
27	
28	\*Among the 3–5% of missing-revenue films that have a US box office figure.
29	
30	**Proposal:** the main analysis keeps the $1M floor. The final model is rerun on the $100K population (7,671 usable films: train 5,554 / test 1,426 / stress 691; 66.9% losers), and the report shows both results side by side. Any $100K result is limited to "films with reported revenue."
31	
32	**Also changes:** the plan adds a step for the $100K sensitivity rerun. `00_build_dataset.ipynb` gets a flag for the $100K population (e.g. `usable_100k`) alongside `usable`.
33	
34	## A3. Label 2.5× as an industry convention
35	**Reason:** 2.5× is a rule of thumb, not something the data shows. Theaters keep roughly half the box office, and marketing often costs about as much as production, so a film needs about 2–2.5× its budget to break even. The report must say that the threshold is an industry convention, cite a source for it, and show the 1×, 2× and 3× sensitivity results next to it.
36	
37	## A4. Inputs: re-open the allowed list (pending)
38	The frozen list allows 8 inputs. The rule behind it stays: **only information known at the financing decision, before production.** The list itself is re-opened. After cleaning, every column that meets the rule is proposed here with its evidence. Candidates so far: MPAA rating, source material, creative type, production method, writer, cast, distributor, franchise / sequel (see `FEATURE_IDEAS.md`).
39	
40	## A5. COVID-era stress test (not discussed yet)
41

# Feature Ideas

A running list of candidate model features for the A10 money-loser screen. Anyone (or their AI) can add to it. Ideas here are **not commitments**: each one still has to pass the contract's time-order rule before it's built.

**Rule for every idea:** the feature may only use information known **at the financing decision, before production**. Nothing from the film's own release or from later films (no box office, scores, reviews, or "how many sequels it eventually got").

**For AI assistants:** whenever a possible feature comes up in conversation, add it here using the template below without waiting to be asked, and tell the user you added it. Don't duplicate an existing idea; add to its notes instead.

## Template

```
### <Short name>
- **Added:** YYYY-MM-DD by <name>
- **Status:** idea | investigating | building | built (notebook §) | rejected (reason)
- **What:** one or two sentences, with an example film
- **Why it might predict a money-loser:**
- **Possible representation:** columns and types
- **Data sources:** which columns in films_unified.csv (or what's missing)
- **Time-order check:** is every input known before production?
- **Open questions:**
```

---

## Ideas

### Sequel / installment number and franchise membership
- **Added:** 2026-11-23 by Tanner
- **Status:** idea
- **What:** Track whether a film belongs to a series of installments and which installment it is, plus whether it belongs to a wider franchise. *Spider-Man* (2002): first installment of the Spider-Man series. *Iron Man* (2008): first installment of the Iron Man series and part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe franchise.
- **Why it might predict a money-loser:** sequels and franchise films come with a built-in audience and earlier box office to compare against, so they likely lose money less often. Late installments may show fatigue.
- **Possible representation:**
  - `is_sequel` (bool): installment number > 1
  - `installment_number` (int): 1, 2, 3, …
  - `in_franchise` (bool) and `franchise_name` (category): wider universe, e.g. MCU
  - `prior_installments` (int): earlier films in the series/franchise released before this one
  - Possibly: the previous installment's performance (multiple of budget), which is known before production
- **Data sources:**
  - The Numbers `tn_Franchise` (already in the unified file; sparse)
  - Wikidata "part of the series" (P179), "series ordinal" (P1545), "follows" (P155). Not pulled yet; would need a new snapshot.
  - TMDB "collections" (`belongs_to_collection`) exist in the TMDB API but **not** in our Kaggle file
- **Time-order check:** ⚠️ "1 **of 3**" leaks the future. When *Spider-Man* (2002) was financed, nobody knew there would be three. Total series length can't be an input; installment number and *prior* installments can.
- **Open questions:**
  - Is the "of N" part usable? Tanner (2026-11-23): installment > 1 is clearly known at financing, and planned series (e.g. announced trilogies) often know their length up front. Debate later; if used, it should be the *planned* length at financing, not the eventual count.
  - Series vs franchise: is *Iron Man 2* installment 2 (Iron Man series) or installment 3 (MCU)? Probably keep both.
  - Reboots and remakes: does *The Amazing Spider-Man* (2012) restart the count?
  - Coverage: how many usable films have franchise data from any source?
