import nbformat
p='notebooks/Edwards-A10.ipynb'
nb=nbformat.read(p,4)
M=nbformat.v4.new_markdown_cell; C=nbformat.v4.new_code_cell
cells=[
M('''## 7. The remaining inputs

Same review as §6 for the other input columns: `fin_budget`, release timing, `mpaa_rating`, `director`, `writer`, `original_language`, `franchise`, `source_material`. Values and spread only; no outcome yet.'''),
M('### 7a. `fin_budget`\n\nThe production budget (the contract allows it as an input). Shown: spread, budget tiers, round-number budgets, and the smallest and largest.'),
C('''b = cu["fin_budget"]
display(numeric_profile(cu, ["fin_budget"]))
profile_grid([(np.log10(b), "log10 fin_budget", "log10 $ (6 = $1M, 8 = $100M)", False)], "films", ncols=1)
btier = pd.cut(b, [0, 5e6, 20e6, 60e6, 150e6, np.inf], labels=["$1-5M", "$5-20M", "$20-60M", "$60-150M", "$150M+"])
display(btier.value_counts().sort_index().rename("films").to_frame().assign(**{"% of films": lambda d: (100 * d["films"] / n_u).round(1)}))
print(f"Budgets that are a round $1M: {(b % 1e6 == 0).mean():.0%}")
print("Source:"); display(cu["fin_budget_src"].value_counts().rename("films").to_frame())
show = ["title", "year", "fin_budget", "fin_budget_src", "runtime_min"]
print("Largest:"); display(cu.nlargest(8, "fin_budget")[show])'''),
M('### 7b. Release timing: `release_date`, `release_month`, `release_quarter`\n\nUS release date, falling back to TMDB\'s first release. Shown: films by month and year, and how often the fallback is used.'),
C('''display(cu["release_date_src"].value_counts().rename("films").to_frame())
rm = cu["release_month"].value_counts().sort_index()
display(pd.DataFrame({"films": rm, "% of films": (100 * rm / n_u).round(1)}).T)
yr = cu["year"].value_counts().sort_index()
display(yr.rename("films").to_frame().T)
rd = pd.to_datetime(cu["release_date"], format="mixed", errors="coerce")
print(f"Release year differs from film year: {(rd.dt.year != cu['year']).mean():.1%} of films")
print("Day of week:"); display(rd.dt.day_name().value_counts().rename("films").to_frame().T)'''),
M('### 7c. `mpaa_rating`\n\nThe Numbers → RT → RT sl, standardized. "NR" (not rated) is a real value; blank means no source had one.'),
C('''mr = cu["mpaa_rating"].value_counts(dropna=False)
display(pd.DataFrame({"films": mr, "% of films": (100 * mr / n_u).round(1)}))
print("Blank by budget tier:")
display(cu["mpaa_rating"].isna().groupby(btier, observed=True).mean().map("{:.0%}".format).rename("% blank").to_frame())
print("Blank by original language (top 6):")
top_lang = cu["original_language"].value_counts().head(6).index
display(cu[cu["original_language"].isin(top_lang)].groupby("original_language")["mpaa_rating"].apply(lambda s: f"{s.isna().mean():.0%}").rename("% blank").to_frame())'''),
M('### 7d. `director` and `writer`\n\nPeople only work as an input as a **track record** (how their earlier films did), so the key question is how many films each person has.'),
C('''for col in ["director", "writer"]:
    v = items(col).value_counts()
    print(f"--- {col}: {len(v):,} distinct people across {cu[col].notna().sum():,} films ---")
    print("People per film:"); display(per_film(col).value_counts().sort_index().head(8).rename("films").to_frame().T)
    print("How many films each person appears in:"); display(films_per_value(col))
    print("Top 10:"); display(v.head(10).rename("films").to_frame().T)
both = cu[["director", "writer"]].dropna()
same = both.apply(lambda r: bool(set(t.strip() for t in r["director"].split(",")) & set(t.strip() for t in r["writer"].split(","))), axis=1)
print(f"Director also credited as writer: {same.mean():.0%} of films with both")'''),
M('### 7e. `original_language`\n\nTMDB → RT, ISO codes.'),
C('''ol = cu["original_language"].value_counts(dropna=False)
display(pd.DataFrame({"films": ol, "% of films": (100 * ol / n_u).round(1)}).head(15))
print(f"{cu['original_language'].nunique()} distinct languages")
print("English vs countries (does the US flag already cover it?):")
us = cu["countries"].fillna("").str.contains("United States")
display(pd.crosstab(cu["original_language"].eq("en").map({True: "English", False: "Not English"}), us.map({True: "includes US", False: "no US"}), margins=True))'''),
M('### 7f. `franchise`\n\nThe Numbers only, split into one value per franchise (`|`-separated). Blank means either "not in a franchise" or "not in The Numbers", and the two can\'t be told apart.'),
C('''fr = cu["franchise"].dropna().str.split("|").explode().str.strip()
frc = fr.value_counts()
print(f"{cu['franchise'].notna().mean():.1%} of films have a franchise; {len(frc):,} distinct franchises")
print("Films per franchise:")
display(pd.cut(frc, [0, 1, 2, 4, np.inf], labels=["1", "2", "3-4", "5+"]).value_counts().sort_index().rename("franchises").to_frame().T)
display(frc.head(15).rename("films").to_frame().T)
print("Filled by budget tier:")
display(cu["franchise"].notna().groupby(btier, observed=True).mean().map("{:.0%}".format).rename("% with franchise").to_frame().T)
print("Franchise vs source_material:")
display(pd.crosstab(cu["source_material"].fillna("(blank)"), cu["franchise"].notna().map({True: "franchise", False: "no franchise"})))'''),
M('### 7g. `source_material`\n\nThe Numbers only.'),
C('''sm = cu["source_material"].value_counts(dropna=False)
display(pd.DataFrame({"films": sm, "% of films": (100 * sm / n_u).round(1)}))
print("Blank by budget tier:")
display(cu["source_material"].isna().groupby(btier, observed=True).mean().map("{:.0%}".format).rename("% blank").to_frame().T)
print(f"source_material and creative_type both blank: {(cu['source_material'].isna() & cu['creative_type'].isna()).mean():.0%}; "
      f"only one blank: {(cu['source_material'].isna() ^ cu['creative_type'].isna()).mean():.0%}")'''),
]
nb.cells.extend(cells)
nbformat.write(nb,p)
EOF

# A10 Purpose Contract: proposed amendments (DRAFT)

Proposed by Tanner Edwards, 2026-11-23. **Not in effect.** These are changes to `A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md`, which was frozen by Matt alone. Each one takes effect only when Tanner and Matt both agree. Agreed items are then copied into the contract's **Amendments** section with the date and reason.

| # | Contract field | Current | Proposed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Population: years | 2000–2023, no reason stated | **Keep 2000–2023**, and record the reason | Proposed |
| A2 | Population: budget floor | Budget ≥ $1M, no sensitivity check | **Keep $1M for the main analysis; rerun at $100K as a sensitivity check.** Budgets under $1K are data errors and are handled in cleaning. | Proposed |
| A3 | Outcome: 2.5× multiple | "Commonly cited rule of thumb" | **Keep 2.5×**, labeled as an industry convention, not a data finding | Proposed |
| A4 | Allowed inputs | Fixed list of 8 | **Re-open after cleaning.** Add every input known at the financing decision. | Open: list to follow |
| A5 | 2020–2023 stress test | COVID years reported separately | Not discussed yet | Open |

## A1. Keep 2000–2023, with a reason
**Reason:** 24 years of films is enough to be relevant to today's market. Before 2000, the data gets thin, and dollar amounts would need inflation adjustment to compare fairly. The end year stays at 2023 because later films hadn't finished their theatrical run when the data was pulled.

## A2. Keep the $1M floor; add a $100K sensitivity check
**Reason to look below $1M:** Low-budget films are part of the financing decision, and they're where the biggest margins happen. Among usable films with a $100K–$1M budget, 14% returned 10× their budget or more, against 4% of films above $1M.

**Reason not to make it the main population:** the S4 rerun (2026-11-23). Revenue is missing far more often below $1M, and the films that are missing it are mostly losers. So the $100K–$1M films we can see lean toward the winners, which probably inflates the 14% figure too.

| Films with a budget | $1M floor | $100K floor | $100K–1M only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Films | 11,212 | 16,065 | 4,853 |
| Missing revenue | 39% | 52% | 83% |
| Missing revenue, 2020–23 | 52% | 69% | 92% |
| Missing-revenue films with US gross < budget* | 98% | 97% | 93% |

\*Among the 3–5% of missing-revenue films that have a US box office figure.

**Proposal:** the main analysis keeps the $1M floor. The final model is rerun on the $100K population (7,671 usable films: train 5,554 / test 1,426 / stress 691; 66.9% losers), and the report shows both results side by side. Any $100K result is limited to "films with reported revenue."

**Also changes:** the plan adds a step for the $100K sensitivity rerun. `00_build_dataset.ipynb` gets a flag for the $100K population (e.g. `usable_100k`) alongside `usable`.

## A3. Label 2.5× as an industry convention
**Reason:** 2.5× is a rule of thumb, not something the data shows. Theaters keep roughly half the box office, and marketing often costs about as much as production, so a film needs about 2–2.5× its budget to break even. The report must say that the threshold is an industry convention, cite a source for it, and show the 1×, 2× and 3× sensitivity results next to it.

## A4. Inputs: re-open the allowed list (pending)
The frozen list allows 8 inputs. The rule behind it stays: **only information known at the financing decision, before production.** The list itself is re-opened. After cleaning, every column that meets the rule is proposed here with its evidence. Candidates so far: MPAA rating, source material, creative type, production method, writer, cast, distributor, franchise / sequel (see `FEATURE_IDEAS.md`).

## A5. COVID-era stress test (not discussed yet)

import nbformat
p='notebooks/Edwards-A10.ipynb'
nb=nbformat.read(p,4)
md='''### 8d. What the outlier checks show (run 2026-11-24), for Tanner's review

**The biggest finding: 929 usable films (14%) exist only in TMDB.** None of The Numbers, Rotten Tomatoes or Box Office Mojo has them, so their budget and revenue (and so the label) come only from TMDB's user-edited data. Almost every other rule mostly catches these same films. They are a mix:
- Junk: *Skibidi Toilet: The Movie*, *Adventures in Bora Bora* ($800M, 5 min), *😤 insect james 😤*, fan edits, concert videos.
- Real films, mostly non-English (80%): *Deep Sea* (China), *Death Note: The Last Name* (Japan), *Solomon Kane*.

| Rule | Films | Proposed |
|---|---|---|
| Runtime 400+ min | 12 | **Exclude.** All TV series or video games (*God of War*, *The Bear*, *What If...?*). |
| Runtime under 60 min | 46 | **Exclude.** Anime episodes, clips, junk. A few real IMAX documentaries (*Sea Rex*), which aren't feature films either. |
| TV Movie genre | 14 | **Exclude.** Not theatrical (*High School Musical*, *Stargate: Continuum*); their revenue figures are made up ($5,940). |
| Title says edition / cut / concert / play | 26 | **Exclude**, except theatrical concert films (*Hannah Montana … Concert*, *Glee: The Concert Movie*). Re-release editions duplicate the real film. |
| Music as the only genre | 15 | **Exclude** if TMDB-only (concert videos). |
| No outside source | 929 | **Decision needed** (below). |
| Budget per minute extreme | 25 | **Exclude.** Junk entries; also shows wrong runtimes on real titles. |
| Non-US $100M+ budget | 12 | **Check by hand.** Some are real US dollars (*The Battle at Lake Changjin*, *Detective Chinatown 3*); *Lost in the Stars* and *Chasing the Dragon* look like local currency. |
| Revenue = budget | 18 | **Exclude.** Copied value, not a real revenue. |
| Revenue under $10K | 101 | Keep if an outside source has the film (real tiny releases, e.g. *The Fanatic*); exclude if TMDB-only. |

**Tanner's Music question:** the Music genre is mostly real films about music (*A Star Is Born*, *Crazy Heart*, *Step Up*, *Footloose*). Concert films that played in theaters (*This Is It*, *Justin Bieber: Believe*) are real releases with real box office. Only the TMDB-only concert videos are junk. **Keep the genre; drop the videos.**

**Budget vs runtime:** works for junk at the edges (5-minute films with $100M budgets) but not in the middle. Budget per minute is roughly flat from 80 to 180 minutes.

**Budget by country:** doesn't show currency errors as a group. China has the highest median ($25M). Currency mistakes are individual films, so they need a hand check, not a country rule.

**New matching problem found:** junk TMDB entries that share a real film's title can take the real film's matches. *WONKA* (2023, "Documentary", 11 min) has 3 outside sources and a $125M budget, and *Wish* (2023, Drama, 66 min) has Disney's $200M budget. The real films may be missing or duplicated. Needs a fix in `00_build_dataset.ipynb`.

**Decision for Tanner: the 929 TMDB-only films**
1. **Exclude all** (recommended). The label can't be checked against anything. Cost: loses some real foreign films and makes the data more US-heavy.
2. **Exclude only those caught by another rule** (about 120). Keeps real foreign films, but leaves unverified revenue in the label.
3. **Keep all**, and add `n_sources` as a data-quality flag for a sensitivity check.

**After this:** §9 goes through missing values one column at a time.
'''
nb.cells.append(nbformat.v4.new_markdown_cell(md))
nbformat.write(nb,p)
EOF

**The main finding: 929 usable films (14%) exist only in TMDB.** None of The Numbers, Rotten Tomatoes or Box Office Mojo has them, so their budget and revenue, and therefore their loser label, can't be checked. Most of the other rules end up catching these same films.
- Some are junk, like *Skibidi Toilet: The Movie*, or *Adventures in Bora Bora* at $800M for 5 minutes.
- Some are real films, mostly non-English (80%).

Apart from that group, the other rules catch 223 films (3.3%). I propose excluding:
- TV series and games
- entries under 60 minutes
- TV movies
- re-release editions and fan cuts
- revenue copied from budget

**Your Music question:** the genre is mostly real films about music, like *A Star Is Born* and *Step Up*. Concert films that played in theaters are real releases. Only the concert videos that exist only in TMDB are junk. So keep the genre and drop those videos.

**Your two budget ideas:** they partly worked.
- **Budget vs runtime:** catches junk at the edges, such as 5-minute "films" with $100M budgets, but not in the middle.
- **Budget by country:** doesn't reveal currency errors as a group. They're individual films, like *Lost in the Stars* and *Chasing the Dragon*, so they need a check by hand.

**A new bug in the build:** the real *Wonka* and *Wish* were still marked "Post Production" in the TMDB snapshot, so the build skipped them. Nothing is committed yet.

**Decision for you: what do we do with the 929 TMDB-only films?**
1. **Exclude them all (my recommendation).** Their label can't be verified. The cost is losing some real foreign films.

# budget/revenue
u['br']=u.fin_budget/u.fin_revenue

content.text:
I recorded "drop everything under 60 minutes." I tested your currency idea first, and it led somewhere slightly different.

**Currency**

The problem with converting is that we don't know which currency a budget was entered in, so there's nothing to convert from. What we can check is where two sources disagree. 3,921 usable films have a budget from both TMDB and The Numbers (or Wikidata):
- 80% agree within 10%.
- Big gaps show up in US films as much as foreign ones. Examples: *Awake* is $86M vs $8.6M, an extra zero; *The Chaser* is $120M vs $2.6M.

So the bigger problem is typos in TMDB's budgets, not currency. The build also uses TMDB's budget first when sources disagree.

**My proposal:**
1. When the two budgets differ by more than 2×, use The Numbers instead of TMDB. That fixes about 70 films with no hand checking.
2. For foreign films with only one budget source, make your scatter plot: budget vs revenue, US vs non-US. Hand-check only the few that sit far out from the rest.

**Revenue under $10K (75 films)**

Your rating idea splits them cleanly:

| Rating | Films |
|---|---|
| Real MPAA rating (R, PG-13, PG, G) | 50 |
| NR | 15 |
| Blank | 10 |

Proposal: keep the 50 rated films as real low grossers, and drop the 25 NR or blank ones.

Do you agree with both proposals?

"""Download the A10 raw datasets from Kaggle into data/raw/.

Run from the repo root:  python tools/get_data.py
Files are gitignored; every collaborator runs this once on their own machine.
data/raw/ is treated as read-only after download — never edit these files.
"""
import shutil
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import truststore

# Use the OS certificate store so downloads work behind TLS-inspecting proxies (e.g. Zscaler)
truststore.inject_into_ssl()

import kagglehub  # noqa: E402

RAW = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "raw"

# Kaggle handle -> (subfolder of data/raw, files expected). Recorded in the Data Receipt.
# stefanoleone992 gets its own subfolder: its rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv shares a
# filename with the (different) andrezaza file Matt's plan already uses.
DATASETS = {
    "asaniczka/tmdb-movies-dataset-2023-930k-movies": ("", ["TMDB_movie_dataset_v11.csv"]),
    "priyamchoksi/rotten-tomato-movie-reviews-1-44m-rows": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv"]),
    "andrezaza/clapper-massive-rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-reviews": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv"]),
    "stefanoleone992/rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-critic-reviews-dataset": (
        "stefanoleone992",
        ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv", "rotten_tomatoes_critic_reviews.csv"],
    ),
    # Scraped from the-numbers.com: budget, domestic/intl/worldwide gross, plus pre-release fields
    "michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata": (
        "the_numbers",
        ["Top Movies (Cleaned Data).csv"],
    ),
}

# Non-Kaggle direct downloads: (subfolder, filename) -> URL
URL_FILES = {
    # Box Office Mojo daily domestic grosses, scraped by github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper
    ("boxofficemojo", "revenues_per_day.csv.gz"):
        "https://github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper/releases/latest/download/revenues_per_day.csv.gz",
}


def main() -> None:
    RAW.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for (subdir, name), url in URL_FILES.items():
        print(f"\n== {url}")
        dst = RAW / subdir / name
        dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        if dst.exists():
            print(f"  exists, skipping: {name}")
            continue
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, dst)
        print(f"  downloaded {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")
    for handle, (subdir, wanted) in DATASETS.items():
        print(f"\n== {handle}")
        src = Path(kagglehub.dataset_download(handle))
        dest_dir = RAW / subdir
        dest_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        for name in wanted:
            dst = dest_dir / name
            if dst.exists():
                print(f"  exists, skipping: {dst.name}")
                continue
            matches = list(src.rglob(name))
            if not matches:
                available = sorted(p.name for p in src.rglob("*") if p.is_file())
                print(f"  NOT FOUND: {name}. Files in download: {available}")
                continue
            shutil.copy2(matches[0], dst)
            print(f"  copied {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    "priyamchoksi/rotten-tomato-movie-reviews-1-44m-rows": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv"]),
    "andrezaza/clapper-massive-rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-reviews": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv"]),
    "stefanoleone992/rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-critic-reviews-dataset": (
        "stefanoleone992",
        ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv", "rotten_tomatoes_critic_reviews.csv"],

    # Scraped from the-numbers.com: budget, domestic/intl/worldwide gross, plus pre-release fields
    "michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata": (

    ),
}

    ("boxofficemojo", "revenues_per_day.csv.gz"):

}


def main() -> None:
    RAW.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for (subdir, name), url in URL_FILES.items():
        print(f"\n== {url}")
        dst = RAW / subdir / name
        dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        if dst.exists():
            print(f"  exists, skipping: {name}")
            continue
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, dst)
        print(f"  downloaded {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")
    for handle, (subdir, wanted) in DATASETS.items():

                print(f"  NOT FOUND: {name}. Files in download: {available}")

content.text:
The test worked for directors and writers but not for distributors. It also turned up a matching bug. I queried 200 films: 100 with blanks to test filling, and 100 complete ones to test accuracy.

| Column | Blanks filled | Agrees with our data | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| director | 12 of 12 | 96% | **Use it** |
| writer | 15 of 18 | 97% | **Use it** |
| runtime | (no blanks in sample) | 96% within 5 min | Use it for the 28 blanks |
| distributor | 12 of 18 | — | **Don't use.** It lists every distributor worldwide plus streamers (Netflix, Hulu, Italy's Eagle Pictures), not the US theatrical one. |
| source_material | 18 of 84 | — | Partial. It only says "based on X"; no entry could mean original or unknown. |
| production_companies | 0 of 3 | — | No help |
| creative_type | — | — | Doesn't exist there |

**The matching bug:** where Wikidata disagreed with us, our row was mixing two different films with the same title:
- *Barbecue* (2014): our director is from an Australian documentary, but the film is a French comedy.
- *Simon* (2004): the same kind of mix.

So the Wikidata comparison doubles as a check for bad matches in the build.

**My recommendation:**
1. Pull director, writer and runtime from Wikidata for all films. That fills about 470 blanks.
2. Flag every film where Wikidata's director disagrees with ours as a possible mismatch, for review.
3. For source material, fill only "based on a book / comic / etc." where Wikidata has it.
4. Leave distributor and creative type blank, with "was missing" flags.

Should I go ahead with the full pull?

"""
import datetime as dt
import json
import time
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import truststore

truststore.inject_into_ssl()

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
QUERY = (ROOT / "tools" / "wikidata_people.rq").read_text()

BATCH = 200


def run(ids: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
    q = QUERY.replace("{IDS}", " ".join(f'"{i}"' for i in ids))
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        "https://query.wikidata.org/sparql",

content.text:
Yes, mostly. TMDB keywords cover 90% of the blanks, and there's good news for your comic-book hypothesis.

**Test:** I grouped the source material into your categories and compared the keywords with The Numbers on 3,801 films where both exist. Overall they agree 74% of the time.

| Keywords say | The Numbers agrees | Blanks this would fill |
|---|---|---|
| Book | 89% | 59 |
| Other adaptation (TV, game, play, toy…) | 89% | 14 |
| Real life | 78% | 85 |
| Comic | 72% (and they find 93% of the real comic films) | 15 |
| Original | 72% | 596 |
| Remake | 50% | 30 |
| No keywords | — | 92 |

**For your hypothesis:** only 15 of the blanks look like comic-book films. The Numbers already covers comic films well, since they're big releases. The blanks are mostly small films.

**The weak spot is "Original."** For films with no source keyword, about 1 in 4 are actually adaptations that nobody tagged. That's 596 of the blanks.

**My proposal:**
1. Add a grouped column, `source_group`, for every film: Comic, Book, Real life, Remake, Other adaptation, Original. This also replaces The Numbers' 23 small categories.
2. Fill the blanks from the keywords.
3. Mark each filled value with where it came from, so we can rerun the model with and without the keyword guesses.

One decision: should the 596 keyword "Originals" be filled as Original, or left as unknown?

    if has("based on comic", "superhero", "based on graphic novel", "based on manga", "comic book", "based on webcomic", "based on cartoon"):
        return "Comic"
    if has("remake", "reboot", "based on movie", "based on short film"):

    if has("based on true story", "biography", "biographical", "based on memoir", "autobiograph"):
